the computation it worries about can no longer start, which I could demonstrate rather than assume. The file builds a 14-variable ideal over ZZ/nextPrime 10000 and annotates numericalIrreducibleDecomposition with 'uses > 20 GB after several hours'. That call is now refused on the spot -- 'expected coefficients that can be converted to complex numbers', NAGtypes.m2:191, in 0.00013 s with no memory movement -- because a numerical method has no business over a finite field. Its first computation still works: groebnerBasis(I, Strategy=>"F4") in 44.1701 s giving 1453 generators at 1.47 GB. Its middle one needs Bertini and about an hour, and was not run. Rebuilding the system over CC, where the method applies, and shrinking it: the ideal is Kuramoto-oscillator equilibria, a circle x_i^2+y_i^2-1 per node with couplings x_i*y_j-x_j*y_i and one normalising linear equation, 2n equations in 2n unknowns with n=7 in the file. At n=2 it returns six points in .433017 s using 7.7 MB; at n=4 it returns dims {0,2} with a degree-14 component in 5.46894 s while RSS falls 23.5 MB. So no leak at any size I could run. n=3 does something else -- see the _numericalID_example.m2 row. Added 2019-05-22 in 4ee798806e, 'bugs in parallel routines applied to NAG and numericalIrreducibleDecomposition', a commit whose only other file is PARALLEL/justin.m2, settled fixed earlier in this catalogue

met by a better mechanism than the one Eisenbud proposed: rather than betti taking two weight vectors and drawing boxes, #906 added MultigradedBettiTally and multigraded(BettiTally), which puts the whole multidegree in each entry as a monomial -- on his own bigraded example multigraded betti gives rows 0,1,2,4 with entries 1, b, a, 2*a*b, a^3*b. That is strictly more information than two projections, and it does not degrade when the numbers reach two digits, which is the worry his message ends on

the ask is met and by the mechanism it names: inverse Matrix routes every InexactField through the engine (matrix1.m2:626 hasEngineLinearAlgebra -> basicInverse -> rawLinAlgInverse -> DMatLinAlg::inverse), whose LU for ARingRR and ARingCC is LAPACK dgetrf_/zgetrf_ (dmat-lu-inplace.hpp:300,348). e4d1989dea routed inexact fields there; 665dab7cbe narrowed it to InexactField so polynomial rings over RR/CC would not use LU. Both predate the PR workflow. Verified: 5x5 random over CC and RR give norm(A*inverse A - I) of 5.6e-16 and 1.7e-15, CC_200 gives 3.9e-60, and the 'experimental computation over inexact field' warning the file quotes now fires only from groebner.cpp:46. But verifying it turned up a live defect in the same function: inverse of a SINGULAR matrix over an inexact field silently returns the zero matrix instead of erroring -- RR_53, CC_53 and RR_200 all do it, while rank, det and solve all report the same matrix singular -- rank is 1, det is -0, and solve(m, id_(RR^2)) returns null, that last being the call inverse makes internally -- so inverse is the only consumer of the LU that reports success. Cause is one line: DMatLinAlg::inverse (dmat-lu.hpp:529) discards solve's bool and returns true unconditionally, though solve returns false at dmat-lu.hpp:379. Inexact fields only: ZZ/5 and ZZ/32003 error correctly via their own ffpack/flint inverse specializations, and ZZ and QQ error on the non-engine quotientRemainder branch. Searched the tracker on ten term sets, ascending, and nothing covers it -- but #2208 is the same ask on ZZ/5, closed by #2241 (a032f77d13), which fixed element-level inversion in ZZp.cpp and aring-zzp*.hpp and never touched dmat-lu.hpp. Distinct from #4506 (non-square, ZZ, non-engine branch, no squareness check) and #3738. Filed as #4556, citing #2208

the ask is 'go the distance to the right of the point in both parts', i.e. carry both parts to a common accuracy, and 530ef987f8 (2008-02-03, 'print complex numbers to a combined precision for both parts') did exactly that on the 1.1 branch -- the release the file asks for it by. It is still the scalar rule: format(...,CC) at gmp1.d:246 derives one accuracy from exponent(z), the larger part, so at printingPrecision 6 a real part more than six decimal places below the imaginary one falls below the printed resolution and 1e-30+ii prints as ii. Matrix and vector entries reach expression CC (reals.m2:494) instead and format the parts independently, so they show | 1e-30+ii |. That difference is not a defect: showing a different number of digits for a CC and for the entry of a matrix over CC is the expected consequence of the two rules, and the scalar rule is the considered one -- a part thirty orders below the other is not part of a six-significant-digit rendering of the number. Note the file's own transcript shows the PRE-530ef987f8 independent formatting, which today's scalar path cannot produce at any printingAccuracy=-1 setting, so the file illustrates one convention while its sentence asks for the other; both halves now show both parts under their own rule

done in 1.3. the syntax the file says is needed already existed when it was written: NewFromMethod dates to the 1997 initial revision (647f7532b3), and every conversion in the file's list installs and runs under it -- 'new List from Matrix := (List,m) -> entries m' then 'new List from matrix{{1,2},{3,4}}' gives {{1,2},{3,4}}, likewise from Set, from Tally, and 'new String from Number' gives a String. The file writes them without 'new', which does not parse, and should not: these expressions construct a new object of type X, so dropping 'new' would not mean anything. What is genuinely unadopted is the speculative block below -- 'Matrix of S from X', 'of' and 'from' as binary operators, 'Scheme over S' -- design sketches from the 2010 Colorado College workshop that nobody pursued, and Core ships none of the specific conversions either, which is a choice rather than a missing mechanism. The file's closing ask, that the 1.3.1.1 parsing precedences be preserved, has held: from/in/of/to/when are still 16 and every level it lists is unchanged. Its one live remnant is the failure it predicts itself: new Matrix from List still falls through to the built-in new HashTable from List and dies with 'key not found in hash table: RawMatrix' at matrix.m2:137 -- the same class of thing as the 'new HashTable from {asdf => foo}' example that opens #4506

fixed by the mechanism the file implies is missing. setup()'s shellfixes carry a third 'rest' field, and MANPATH's is ':' (files.m2:442), which the bash template drops into the empty case as VAR="/PREFIX/DIR:REST" -> MANPATH="/prefix/man:" (files.m2:412). A trailing colon is precisely what BSD and macOS man read as 'and then the default path from man.conf', so the defaults the file worries about losing are preserved rather than replaced. still true and deliberately so. orP(constParser "&&", constParser "&") on input "&" throws: it commits to && and cannot back off. But the absence of backtracking is a design decision stated in the source -- andP carries the comment 'we don't do backtracking: the first parser absorbs as much as it can, and then the second one takes over' (Parsing.m2:97) -- and the package's own tests assert the resulting failures, expecting parser(orP(NNParser, constParser "ab"), "a") and the "abc" case to throw (Parsing.m2:547-550). Changing it would break the package's tests by design. The file's other half, 'doesn't work as advertised', is nearly met: the orP doc now states the requirement, 'In an efficient grammar, the first token presented to r will be acceptable to at most one of the input parsers'. Residual nit only, not worth an issue: the Outputs line above it still promises a parser accepting anything acceptable to one of them, without the caveat. Also worth noting the file's own reproducer is unusable as written -- orP("&", "&", "a") is HTML-escaped, so what was tested cannot be recovered from the text

1/3 == 1./3 is still false, and it is the right answer. The comparison is exact, not a promotion: compare(x:RR, y:QQ) is mpfr_cmp_q (gmp.d:1475-1479), which compares the double against the rational without rounding either, and since the nearest double to 1/3 is below 1/3 the result is 1/3 > 1./3, which M2 reports. Dan's proposed fix, making them compare equal, would require rounding the rational to the float's precision first -- that is what would make == inexact, and it would break transitivity against nearby rationals. Where the float is exact the two do agree: 1/2 == 0.5 and 1/4 == .25 are both true, which is the tell that promotion is not what is happening. mpfr_cmp_q predates the file (510344c38c, 2008-01), so nothing changed here and the answer to the file's closing question, 'Is it okay?', was settled by leaving it alone

not installed: R_(1..3) still errors with 'no method for binary operator _' on (PolynomialRing, Sequence). Two spellings do the job today -- (R_*)_{1,2,3} and, literally the file's own body, apply(1..3, i -> R_i), both giving (b,c,d) -- so this is convenience rather than a gap in capability. One detail for whoever takes it: the adjacent slot is already occupied and differently, since R_{1,2,3} means the monomial with that exponent vector, a*b^2*c^3, so Ring _ List is not available but Ring _ Sequence is free. R_* postdates the file and covers most of what David liked about it. #3515 is a different notation ask, about partial application of functions

all three of Mike's numbered problems are settled, and the Riemann-Roch formula Sheldon asked for comes out exactly. (3), the one Mike called a bug -- chi L giving terms of degree above dim X -- is gone: on X = base(3, Bundle=>(L,1,D), Bundle=>(T,3,b)) with X.TangentBundle = T, part_3(todd X * ch L) contains only degree-3 monomials, mechanically checked, and chi L is integral(1/6 D_1^3 + 1/4 D_1^2 b_1 + 1/12 D_1 b_1^2 + 1/12 D_1 b_2 + 1/24 b_1 b_2). That is the Maple output in the file term for term under -K = b_1 and c2 = b_2. (1) and (2), which Mike called cosmetic -- naming the class D rather than D_1, and chern T = 1 - K + c_2 + c_3 -- work through the route he proposed himself in his third email: abstractSheaf(Y, Rank=>3, ChernClass=>1-K+c_2+c_3) prints chern TT as exactly 1 - K + c_2 + c_3, and part_3(todd Y * ch M) gives 1/6 D^3 - 1/4 D^2 K + 1/12 D*K^2 + 1/12 D*c_2 - 1/24 K*c_2. base itself still always subscripts, b_1..b_n (Schubert2.m2:399). And chi M, which his email says fails because integral is unknown there, now returns the integral. No fix commit pinned: this arrived as continued development of Schubert2, not as a response to the file

cached now, and by fixing the cause Dan suspected. He guessed the gb was not cached 'perhaps because the module is not', and his peek I.cache showed only generators; today it shows {module, generators}, so the module is cached on the ideal. The gb itself lands in (generators I).cache under a GroebnerBasisOptions{HardDegreeLimit => null, Syzygies => false, SyzygyRows => 0} key and is reused -- on a 7-generator monomial ideal in 8 variables the second gb call is about 4.6x faster than the first. gb MonomialIdeal still resolves to the generic gb Ideal := opts -> I -> gb(module I, opts) at gb.m2:311, exactly as in his transcript, so nothing needed a MonomialIdeal-specific method; caching the module was enough. No fix commit pinned

two live asks, one of them a verified documentation defect. The thread opens with Mike reporting that 'our description of how to remove a cached GB is no longer correct', and that description is still in the manual: ov_groebner_bases.m2:439 is an EXAMPLE block that says 'we must erase the memory of the Groebner basis computed above', runs remove(f.cache,{false,0}), then says 'compute the Groebner basis anew' and times it. The key is a GroebnerBasisOptions hash today, not {false,0}, so that remove is a silent no-op -- verified: keys (generators I).cache is unchanged across it and the gb is still cached -- which means the timing the manual displays for the Hilbert-hint computation is a cache hit rather than a fresh run. The two gbRemove copies at ov_rings.m2:1535-1536 carry the same stale key but sit inside -* *- blocks, so they are dead. The design half is unadopted and undecided: gb and res have no UseCache, Cache or CleanCache option, clearCache exists nowhere in Core (only as a BasicDivisor method in WeilDivisors), and Mike's getGroebnerKey never appeared -- though the key is at least inspectable now via keys (generators I).cache. Filed as one issue covering both halves on the maintainer's call

addressed, and the comment left behind names this exact problem. libraries/gfan/Makefile.in:12-13 reads 'Inject LDFLAGS via CDD_LINKOPTIONS so the linker can find cddlib (homebrew on macOS, system or M2-built elsewhere)', and passes CDD_LINKOPTIONS="$(LDFLAGS) -lcddgmp" so the link step follows whatever cddlib configure selected; cddlib is in LIBLIST (configure.ac:590) so --with-system-libs covers it, and configure.ac:609-611 records that both gfan and topcom depend on it. check loads the documentation itself now, which is precisely the ask. the premise is a 32-bit-by-default toolchain on 64-bit-capable Intel hardware, which is how Mac OS X 10.5 and 10.6 shipped. configure.ac has no sysctl, no hw.optional and no -m64 anywhere, and it needs none: every supported Mac is 64-bit, Apple Silicon has no 32-bit userland at all, and the compilers default to 64-bit, so the automatic --build=x86_64-apple-darwin CC="gcc -m64" the file asks for would now be either a no-op or wrong. done, by the autoconf idiom rather than by version arithmetic: where a particular version is needed, configure either checks the version or checks for the feature that version brought, and the second is the normal case. configure.ac carries 107 feature-test invocations -- 34 AC_SEARCH_LIBS, 34 AC_CHECK_HEADER, 14 AC_COMPILE_IFELSE, 11 AC_LINK_IFELSE, 10 AC_CHECK_HEADERS, 7 AC_RUN_IFELSE and so on -- including compile-and-link probes against flint, givaro, gmp and libnormaliz headers, which is exactly 'checking that recent versions appear' expressed as what the code needs rather than as a number. Explicit version gates exist for the two cases where no feature test would do: GNU make 3.81 is rejected at :209, and Arb errors 'found but too old' at :902. Separately, anything M2 builds itself is version-exact -- 27 of 37 libraries/*/Makefile.in pin a VERSION with a SHA256SUM. Recorded first as open on a count of version comparisons, which was the wrong measurement: a low count of those is what a well-written configure script looks like, not evidence of a gap

a non-goal rather than a gap, and the ecosystem settled it the other way. getWWW is a hand-rolled HTTP/1.1 client from 1996 (http.m2, Copyright 1996) that writes request lines onto a socket with four headers, and delegates HTTPS to a subprocess -- 'openssl s_client -quiet -verify 1' at http.m2:45-48. It is a plain method() with no options, so there is nowhere to pass a cookie, and nothing reads Set-Cookie. But no consumer wants one: OnlineLookup does stateless query-string GETs against oeis.org/search and wayback.cecm.sfu.ca/cgi-bin/isc/lookup, and ReflexivePolytopesDB the same against quark.itp.tuwien.ac.at/cgi-bin/cy/cydata.cgi. That package also shows what happened instead: it carries a documented Access option taking 'm2', 'curl' or 'wget' (ReflexivePolytopesDB.m2:93-98), so an author who hit getWWW's limits shelled out rather than asking for the feature -- and curl brings cookies, redirects, TLS, proxies and auth together, each of which getWWW would otherwise reimplement, cookies being the first of the sequence rather than the last. The second ask, 'also the email address option!', is two words that cannot be reconstructed from the file; the likeliest reading is a From: header, but nothing in the tree corroborates it and guessing was not worth publishing. Would be worth revisiting only for a concrete endpoint someone wants that requires a cookie

reproduces, and it is not merely counter-intuitive as the file says -- it contradicts the documentation. ov_debugging.m2:102-107 promises that after typing end, 'the debugger will be entered again ... at the point inside the function g from which the function f was called', and that listLocalSymbols will then show g's local variables. Side by side on 1.26.06: with the file's functions, which declare no locals, end returns straight to the top-level prompt and g is never entered. With the same call structure but a local variable in each function, end re-enters the debugger inside the caller and listLocalSymbols shows it. both halves settled, and the second one exactly. a design musing that was never taken up, and the file knows it -- it ends 'Feedback on that idea would be welcome'. The description still holds: degree of the zero ring element is -infinity, while a zero vector keeps the degree of whatever it came from, so degree(0*F_1) is {0}. The proposal was to make R seriously graded with distinct zero elements of each degree, and the file itself names the reason nobody did: you would then have to decide whether r == s and r === s agree for zeros of different degrees, which is a change to equality semantics across the whole system for a cosmetic gain. Fifteen years on there is one zero per ring and no sign anyone wants otherwise

done, and my first reading was wrong. I checked class degreeLift, found an unbound Symbol, and recorded the ask unmet -- but the feature is not a global function of that name, it is a derivation inside map. ringmap.m2:97-104 builds degmapmatrix from the DegreeMap and, when the user supplies no DegreeLift, derives one by solving quotientRemainder against it, raising 'degreeLift: degree not liftable' where no lift exists; identity is short-circuited. Verified: for map(A,B,gens A,DegreeMap => reverse) the cache holds a DegreeLift FunctionClosure at ringmap.m2:101 which sends {1,0} to {0,1}, correctly inverting reverse, and a map with no DegreeMap gets identity. So 'we can compute the degreeLift function for the user automatically' is exactly what map now does. #2580, DegreeLift not preserving homogeneity for multigraded maps, still reproduces and is a separate live bug in the same mechanism

same root cause as #3557, 'rank fails over ZZ because codim needs Generic => true', by way of a different entry point. Re-checked case by case rather than in a batch, and the four cases do not fail the same way: ideal(2) alone is an ideal of ZZ, so A/ideal(2) errors 'expected ideal of the same ring' at the quotient, which is arguable rather than wrong; but ideal(2,x), ideal(two) and ideal(two,x) are all ideals of A, those quotients build fine, and every dim on them fails with the identical message 'codim: expected an affine ring (consider Generic=>true to work over QQ)'. So the answers Bart Snapp wanted (A/2 is (ZZ/2)[x], dimension 1) are blocked by the same plumbing that blocks rank. Neighbours over ZZ, none of them this: #4095 trim, #1518 kernels of ring maps. Settled by commenting on #3557

the need has a one-line answer already. dismiss on a PolynomialRing still reports no method, as in the transcript, but the file's stated purpose is the tentative sentence after it -- 'This could unassign x, releasing it for other uses...' -- and that is what 'x = symbol x' does: verified, after QQ[y] the symbol y has class the ring, after y = symbol y it is a Symbol again, and QQ[y] can be built afresh. the same puzzle as #1477, 'Dispatching of lift and promote', which asks why lift's method is installed the way it is, observes that Ring is not among RingElement's ancestors so the dispatch is hard to account for, and concludes 'the documentation is rather thin in this area'. reproduces byte for byte and the cause is one line. net Superscript (expressions.m2:774-779) raises the exponent by 1 + depth n, computed from the exponent's own net, so the offset ignores how tall the base is; the parenthesized quotient ring measures (height, depth) = (3,3), six lines with its baseline in the middle, and the exponent lands on row 2 of 6 exactly as the file's arrow marks. Raising by max(1 + depth n, height b) against the base net puts it above the top line, which is what the file asks for, and is byte-identical to today for a one-line base and for a matrix base -- checked, since the tempting height b - 1 breaks the ordinary case by dropping the exponent onto the baseline. unmet on all three counts and data is genuinely lost, measured rather than read: after zzf << "hello"; zzf = null and two collectGarbage() calls the file is empty and openFiles() still lists it. At normal exit it does reach disk, via closem (d/stdio.d:575-583) registered with atend -- which flushes but does not close. Two blockers, and the second is the interesting one. There is no finalizer on the file type (git grep -i finaliz over d/stdio0.d d/stdio.d d/stdiop.d exits 1; every GC_REGISTER_FINALIZER in the tree is for foreign pointers, mysql, pthreads or engine objects). And openfiles (d/stdio.d:154-158) is a strong-reference list that addfile pushes every file onto and only rmfile removes, from cleanUp, after close -- so an unclosed file is reachable from a GC root and can never be collected, which is what openFiles() still listing it demonstrates. The two halves of the file are in tension: the flush-at-exit net that makes the common case work depends on that same pinning. #1515 is a hard second blocker, registerFinalizer broken since <=1.12 with #2728 on the same GC warnings and #1852 closed as its duplicate

filed as one issue covering the whole for-bounds gap, with 1-for-sequence-idea and 1-for-by as duplicates of it. Bart Snapp's example still fails: for i from (0,0) to (5,6) gives 'expected an integer' while the form the file compares it to, for j in (0,0)..(5,6), iterates all nine pairs -- verified. evalForCode (d/evaluate.d:314) is the whole story. And there is no step at all: forCode (d/parse.d:252) has inClause, fromClause, toClause, whenClause, listClause and doClause and no field for one, and "by" appears nowhere in the d sources as a keyword -- which is why 1-for-by's first example fails as 'no method for adjacent objects: 0 (of class ZZ) SPACE by (of class Symbol)' rather than as a for-loop error. So the loop body already handles what the bounds refuse, and both needs are reachable today through the in clause: for i in reverse(0..4) descends, for i in select(0..10, zzk -> zzk%2==0) steps, both verified. merged into #4580, filed from 1-for-loop-idea.m2, the same ask from a second reporter: for i from (1,1,1,1,1,1) to (1,2,3,4,5,6) gives 'expected an integer' because the from and to clauses take only a small integer (d/evaluate.d:348-358) while the in clause takes any iterable. the two resource-limit steps shipped and the security content is better done from outside the process. Of the seven-step recipe, step 1 is limitFiles and step 6 is limitProcesses (d/system.d:204-221, documented ov_system.m2:2044-2062), both from 778e7f0cad (2012-03-13) -- the same commit as the --read-only-files the file itself credits, which still works: openOut under it is blocked. Steps 2-5, the privilege separation, are absent; there is no chroot or setuid anywhere in d/, c/ or e/, and class sandbox is Symbol. Two reasons not to pursue it. The recipe is fork-then-drop-privileges and fork's own documentation now says very few operations can be safely done in the child of a multithreaded program, even allocating memory -- M2 became multithreaded after this was written. And sandboxing the whole M2 process externally is strictly better than building privilege separation in: a container runtime, systemd unit confinement, a seccomp or firejail-style wrapper or a VM all cover the engine and every library M2 links, do not depend on M2 being correct about it, and need no fork inside a threaded process. Macaulay2Web is one consumer that does exactly that, out of tree. A judgment, so overrule it cheaply. One live gap that is not this file's ask: --read-only-files is documented nowhere in Macaulay2Doc or the man page, unlike limitFiles and limitProcesses. #519 is the adjacent resource-limits issue

works now, and correctly for the case that can be correct. frac(QQ[x]/x^2[y]) returns a FractionField instead of 'not implemented yet: fraction fields of polynomial rings over rings other than ZZ, QQ, or a finite field', because 711507e071 (pzinn, 2024-02-27, PR #3177 'frac of iterated ring') made factoryAlmostGood recurse through the whole chain (enginering.m2:335-342) where it previously looked only one level down at coefficientRing and so refused iterated rings wholesale. The guard at enginering.m2:350 is still there; it was widened, not removed. For a domain base it is sound: over frac((QQ[a]/(a^2-2))[y]), a^2 == 2, y*(1/y) == 1, 1/a*a == 1 and (y+a)/(y+a) == 1. Found while checking this, and NOT filed here because it is the live core of bugs/mike/0-frac-bug, still todo: the same guard never asks whether any quotient in the chain is prime, so frac accepts non-domains and builds a ring that is not one. frac's own documentation says the input is an integral domain. In frac(ZZ[t]/(t^4)) -- 0-frac-bug's ring -- t =!= 0, t^4 == 0, t*(1/t) == 1 and yet (t^4)*(1/t) == 0 while t^3*(t*(1/t)) == t^3, so the same product grouped two ways gives 0 and t^3. That file's own transcript is fixed, its product l now being 1 rather than a nilpotent denominator, so it could have been settled fixed on the symptom Filed as #4576 and bugs/mike/0-frac-bug settled as its duplicate.

Exception (a), a Hilbert hint for res, is still literally as Dan describes: options gb has Hilbert and options res does not, comp-res.hpp and comp-res.cpp contain no hilbert at all, and set_hilbert_function exists only on GB classes. Demonstrated by installing a deliberately wrong hint, poincare J = 1: gens gb J becomes the zero map, so gb used it, while betti res J is unchanged from the correct resolution. res is now a synonym for Complexes' freeResolution, and the front-end store exists (poincare M = p, hilbert.m2:110) with no resolution consumer. Exception (b) is unmet too: isHomogeneous has 12 methods and none takes more than one argument, so there is no way to ask about the first degree component alone; Complexes/FreeResolution.m2:215-380 substitutes heft R =!= null, which is weaker, and full multigraded isHomogeneous, and does not enforce Mike's 'algorithm 3 additionally singly graded'. Filed as one issue covering both exceptions. #4487 is adjacent to (b), #3937 is why canUseHilbertHint was hardened

unmet, and the answer is cheaper than the file imagined -- reframed onto FLINT, since PARI left the tree in e79bd82855 (2025-03-07). findGalois (galois.m2:95-121) asks a hook, the only hook is ConwayPolynomials, and its data is FLINT's Conway table (ConwayPolynomials.m2:13, 'the data comes libflint', via a2fd44e9f0). Outside that table it falls to galois.m2:113, a brute-force search over dense random monic polynomials, then findPrimitive. Measured: conwayPolynomial(3,100) is null, GF(3,100) takes 6.5s then 4.8s and yields a 67-term modulus that differs on every call, while rawConwayPolynomial(3,100,true) -- FLINT's fq_nmod_ctx_init -- returns a modulus with 3 nonzero coefficients in 2.2ms. ConwayPolynomials.m2:16 hard-codes false, so GF never sees it. GF(3,582), the pari thread's own example, does not finish at all in any practical sense: left running without a timeout it was still going after 55 minutes at 99 percent of a core and 261MB, and was killed rather than completing. Two aggravating details: the modulus is non-deterministic, so GF(3,100) in two sessions gives incompatible fields, and findPrimitive (galois.m2:118) is computed then discarded on the FlintBig path (galois.m2:174-181), i.e. wasted precisely in the slow cases. Coupled cost for whoever takes it: a non-Conway modulus makes map(GaloisField,GaloisField) error by design (ConwayPolynomials.m2:42), which is #2143. #1917 is adjacent, same galois.m2 block

Dan asked to get it to work and then made it work, within weeks. 318dccabbd (2008-10-22, 'GF gcd now working'), after eeb878da6d ('GF gcd progress') and 89ed026e2e ('start interface with Singular Libfac for factorization over finite non-prime fields'), added the modeGF branch that calls set_GF_minimal_poly, now at e/interface/factory.cpp:515-519 inside rawGCDRingElement. Verified on the file's own input: A = GF(3,20, Variable => a), R = A[x], gcd(F,G) returns a cubic that divides both F and G and is an associate of the expected common factor a*x^3-2*a*x^2-x-1 -- degree 3, remainder zero both ways, leadCoefficient ratio exact. The file's second half, the toField comparison it says should work, is the part that is still broken; that belongs to bugs/mike/0-gcd-doc.m2, whose last block is this file's example verbatim

no longer recursive, so the limit cannot be reached. gcd(500:1) and lcm(500:1) both return 1, and gcd(5000:1) does too. Binary associative methods now fold iteratively: foldL (methods.m2:72) is (f, x, L) -> (scan(L, y -> x = f(x, y)); x), used by the Sequence and List dispatch installed at methods.m2:87-90, so argument count costs no stack depth. That shape reached its current form in PR #1939 (43cc816c41 and 6e85628c9e, February 2021), but the pre-#1939 code was already a for loop rather than a recursion, so the recursive version the file hit is older; the loop first appears in 5598a53088, a February 2009 merge of r8149-r8463 from the 1.2 release branch, which is the era of this file. fix left blank because that is a branch merge rather than a targeted commit, and pinning the original would need a bisect

unmet, and instead of declining it gcd returns a common divisor that is not greatest. Over QQ[a]/(a^2-1), which is QQ x QQ, with e = (1+a)/2 and f = (1-a)/2 verified idempotent and orthogonal: for F = e*(x-1)+f*(x-2) and G = e*(x-1)+f*(x-3), d = e*(x-1)+f has degree 1 and divides both, yet gcd(F,G) is 1. My first example, (x^2-1)*(x-a) against (x^2-1)*(x+a), gave the right answer x^2-1 and was a coincidence -- both components share a gcd there. Cause identified and the capability already exists: gcd calls the two-argument rawGCD (factor.m2:26-28) with no minimal polynomial, so an extension in the coefficient ring is invisible and only the base-field part comes back. Over K = QQ[a]/(a^6-a^3-1) with R = K[t], F = t^6-t^3-1 and G = (t-a)*(t+a), t-a divides both and the front end says 1, while rawGCD(raw F, raw G, raw (ideal K)_0) returns t-a. That is Mike's 2009 diagnosis verbatim, bugs/mike/0-gcd-doc.m2 line 3, 'rawGCDRingElement is not being called from the front end'. Also: the guard Dan proposed in #321 -- 'just give an error if the ring is a quotient ring' -- exists at factor.m2:24 but tests only the top ring, so gcd errors in QQ[a]/(a^2-1) and proceeds in (QQ[a]/(a^2-1))[x], and likewise for pzinn's own ZZ[y]/(y^2+3) example. Third guard-depth defect of this cohort after #4576 and #4578. bugs/mike/0-gcd-doc.m2 is left todo on purpose: it is a 120-line multi-ask file covering factor over toField ('NOT CORRECT!!'), bivariate gcd and missing documentation, so it must be read against this issue rather than settled as its duplicate. #1958 is the units-in-a-field case Mike called expected

duplicate of #4179, which owns the behaviour that would explain it. The file is one dead 2009 URL, http://online.wsj.com/xml/rss/3_7041.xml, and the words 'This doesn't work', so the original cause cannot be verified -- but getWWW returns the raw response including the status line and never parses it, which is #4179's first point. met, in a better place than the file asked for. There is no such check in configure.ac -- every gmp test there is presence or version, including the only AC_RUN_IFELSE at :918-940, which is a compile-time __GNU_MP_VERSION predicate. But tests/normal/random.m2 is exactly this test: its first line is '-- let's make sure the random number generator doesn't change', and it pins the output of random 100 and of five seed settings against hard-coded vectors, with the superseded pre-1.1 vectors left in comments as the record of the last change. It runs in both build systems and therefore in CI, and it passes today against gmp 6.3.0 -- verified by loading it under --no-randomize, which is how the harness runs tests and which the file's own lines 3-5 explain. M2 does depend on gmp here: random ZZ reaches mpz_urandomm on a gmp_randinit_default state (e/interface/random.cpp:25,63), and gmp documents that default as free to change between releases. A configure probe would be strictly worse -- it cannot see M2's own seeding layer and would fire on machines that only consume prebuilt packages. Residue not filed: random QQ and random RR (random.cpp:182-183, :217, :245, the latter via mpfr_urandomb) have no pinned vectors

decided by the file's own author, twice. 511504951f (2009-03-27, eight days after the file) implemented exactly this -- 'change caching of example outputs so the hash code is not dependent on the type List', switching the stored value to toSequence -- and 7c41af8e0e (2009-10-06) reverted it, 'change stored example inputs back to a list, instead of a sequence / be prepared to fix the resulting problems', leaving a standing instruction that survives verbatim at examples.m2:165-166: 'don't convert "ex" on the next line to a sequence, because the hash code for caching example outputs will change'. The rationale also fails on inspection: hash's own documentation (ov_hashtables.m2:913-917) names lists and sequences in one clause at the same weak guarantee, 'will be avoided, if possible', and hash List and hash Sequence are 1000041 and 1000042, adjacent draws from one type counter, so the swap buys no stability. the cited idea does not apply to M2's design, and the measurable headroom is negligible. Brent's paper is about shortening probe sequences in open-addressed scatter storage; M2 uses separate chaining -- KeyValuePair is {key, hash, value, next} at d/parse.d:463 -- and hashtables.dd:137-142 records that new entries are prepended deliberately, because appending 'might cause a reader to encounter the same key twice' for readers that do not lock the table. Adopting open addressing would mean discarding that lock-free-reader invariant. Measured over 10^6 operations against a 0.372s interpreter floor: MutableHashTable store 0.723s and lookup 0.660s against MutableList 0.342s and 0.451s, so a hash lookup is about 1.5x an array index end to end and is dominated by interpreter dispatch rather than probing; a collision-free table could save tens of nanoseconds per operation. No issue among 4600+ has ever reported hash-table speed, the paper's URL in the file is a mangled Google redirect that no longer resolves, and the note names no symptom, benchmark or threshold. A judgment, so overrule it cheaply. #2591 was about hash-code quality rather than table structure

duplicate of #1608, where Dan restated this ask himself in 2020 with the rationale the one-line file lacks: 'much more useful ... would be to implement red-black trees, which are a type of height balanced trees, where the keys can be any objects of Macaulay2 for which ? provides a total ordering'. Commented there rather than filed, because the comment's contribution is that the premise fails three ways, measured: ? is partial (1 ? "a", symbol x ? 1 and {1} ? (1,) all give 'no method'), it can answer 'incomparable' for Sets rather than one of < = >, and #650 still reproduces so it is unstable where it does answer -- sort applied twice to a list of Sets alternates between two orders. So a balanced-tree type cannot take 'any objects for which ? is a total order' as its key domain; it needs a comparison supplied at construction, or a documented restriction, or #650 fixed first. Current state for the record: Core has no ordered container at all, and no distributed package implements one

the premise is measurably false. One help call costs nothing: M2 -q -e 'help merge' peaks at 125148KB against a 125312KB do-nothing baseline, i.e. inside run-to-run noise; 200 help nodes cost +3MB; and about("merge", Body => true), which opens every installed database and reads every value, costs +7MB. There is no 'whole help is read in' event, because documentation lives in per-package databases opened on demand and memoized (system.m2:352-354) and retrieved one key at a time, with the value only evaluated at that moment (document.m2:379-381). The debug-mode limit the email is about still exists and was doubled for debug builds in 230286b1f5 (2021-06-26): run.m2:114-116 sets GC_MAXIMUM_HEAP_SIZE=800M when --enable-debug appears in the configure arguments and 400M otherwise, and Dan's own follow-up 76361ca44c (2011-02-19) raised the example limits five months after this file. Two things unverified: the 800M branch, since neither M2 available here is an --enable-debug build, and whether ulimit -m at run.m2:13 is the no-op on Linux that RLIMIT_RSS semantics suggest. #1879 is a different phenomenon, bdwgc heap fragmentation during html generation on i386

no leak, measured rather than inspected. Max RSS is flat across iteration counts -- 303300KB at n=1, then 305076, 304948, 304848 and 304824KB at n=5, 10, 20 and 40 -- against a 124672KB do-nothing baseline and 125048KB for building the matrix alone. So the first hermite call costs about 178MB of one-time working set and every subsequent call costs nothing, which is the opposite of the file's claim. Wall time scales linearly at roughly 0.9s per 30x30 Hermite normal form, so the file's own scan(1000, ...) would take about 17 minutes; that is a separate complaint the file does not make. fix blank: nothing identifies when it stopped leaking. bugs/mike/0-gauss-hermite.m2 and bugs/mike/1-hermiteLLL-leadTerm are unread neighbours in the same area

Dan answered his own question the same day he asked it. The file is his 2008-12-10 email -- 'For a projective variety hilbertFunction() simply applies itself to the underlying graded ring. Similarly for coherent sheaves. This might be unexpected behavior. Should we fix it?' -- with Eisenbud's reply 27 minutes later saying the right answer for a sheaf is the Hilbert function of the global section module, via Hom(mm^d, M) with d from the Castelnuovo-Mumford regularity, and asking 'Worth including automatically?'. 8b32397e67, committed that same day, is 'disable hilbertFunction etc. on projective varieties': the method ae25d821e5 had added in 2000 (hilbertFunction(ZZ,CoherentSheaf) delegating to F.module) gained a notImplemented() guard, and 2964a771ad (2021-11-23) removed it altogether. Today hilbertFunction has nine methods, none for CoherentSheaf or ProjectiveVariety, and both error with 'no method found'. Eisenbud's global-sections capability was never added. hilbertPolynomial still delegates the naive way for both (Varieties.m2:198 and :361), which the file itself calls okay and which CoherentSheaf equality depends on at :376. The file's other pointer is stale: only one 'temporarily disabled' remains in the tree, at help.m2:305, and it is about broken links

reproduces byte for byte: with A = QQ[a], B = QQ[b] and C = A**B, substitute(vars A, C) gives isHomogeneous false and degrees {{{0,0}},{{0,0}}} while degrees C is {{1,0},{0,1}}. The file's own framing is right -- 'if only substitute would pay attention to how C was constructed from A' -- and the information is derivable: map(C,A) carries no DegreeMap, and supplying the obvious one, map(C, A, {C_0}, DegreeMap => d -> d | {0}), makes it homogeneous with degrees {{{0,0}},{{1,0}}}. The tensor already computes it. monoids.m2:692 applies d -> join(d,N0) to the first factor's degrees inline and :694 stores only the second factor's map as opts.DegreeMap. I predicted from that asymmetry that substitute(vars B, C) would work where vars A fails; it does not, both are non-homogeneous with zero degrees, so the stored map is not consulted either and the fix is to plumb it rather than to add the missing half. Second row of this session where the needed information exists and the front end does not use it, after #4583's minimal polynomial. #2905 is the adjacent tensor-and-degrees bug that three settled rows already point at

filed as the general gap rather than the D-module one. the collision the file describes cannot happen, guarded three ways. The generated header is include/M2/config.h (configure.ac:4), not include/config.h, and every M2 site includes it namespaced -- d/types.h:1 and e/engine-includes.hpp:10 use <M2/config.h>, c/scc.h:3 uses "M2/config.h" -- so CPPFLAGS=-I/tmp/foo with /tmp/foo/config.h cannot shadow it; the builder would have to create /tmp/foo/M2/config.h deliberately. Even then there is a sentinel: configure.ac:524 defines M2_CONFIG_H with the comment 'a macro definition to ensure our config.h was the one loaded' and d/types.h:2-3 raises #error without it. And the flag order the file asks for is in place: config.Makefile.in:70-74 prepends -I@abs_top_srcdir@/include, -I@abs_top_builddir@/include and -I$(BUILTLIBPATH)/include ahead of the builder's $(CPPFLAGS), with d/Makefile.in:170 carrying the comment "it's important that *our* directories get searched first". d/ and e/ do differ, but in M2_CPPFLAGS placement, which holds only -D flags -- last in d/Makefile.in:171 and first in e/Makefile.common.in:4 -- so a builder passing -UNDEBUG would be overridden in one and win in the other. That is a separate, small inconsistency with a clean closing condition, recorded rather than filed. Residual hole outside the file's scope: make CPPFLAGS=... on the command line still clobbers the chain, which config.Makefile.in:58-60 acknowledges

it does something definite now: it errors. R = QQ[u,u] then R_"u" gives 'variable not found in ring' rather than the random generator the file reports, and it errors consistently across repeated calls. String indexing itself is unharmed -- on a ring with distinct names S_"v" returns v, and a name that is absent errors the same way. So the ask, 'it should do something more definite', is met. One wrinkle worth noting for whoever touches the message: for QQ[u,u] the name is not absent but ambiguous, so 'variable not found in ring' describes the situation imprecisely even though refusing is right

the need is served and the change would cost more than it buys. InfiniteNumber is still a type and class infinity is still InfiniteNumber, so the ask is unmet -- but the bridge it asks for exists: numeric infinity returns an RR, and numeric_100 infinity honours a precision, so 'an infinite real of the current defaultPrecision' is available on demand. What the file proposes beyond that is abolishing the symbolic class, and that class is load-bearing as a sentinel: options res carries LengthLimit => infinity, SyzygyLimit => infinity and PairLimit => infinity, compared against integers, and #3656 uses infinity the same way. Collapsing it into an RR would change what those comparisons mean across the tree. The friction the proposal would remove is real and tracked -- #1597, open since 2020, still reproduces exactly: infinity * 0_RR is 0 while (1/0_RR) * 0_RR is NotANumber and infinity * 0_R errors outright -- but that issue asks for consistency rather than unification. A judgment, so overrule it cheaply

the investigation the file asks for has a definite answer, and it is yes. dpkg handles it structurally rather than per package: install-info declares 'interest-noawait /usr/share/info' as a file trigger, /usr/share/info/dir is owned by no package and maintained by that trigger, and macaulay2-common needs no .triggers file of its own -- dpkg fires install-info's whenever any package adds or removes files there. The entries are present here, /usr/share/info/dir carrying 24 Macaulay2 lines including '* Macaulay2Doc: (Macaulay2Doc). Macaulay2 documentation', and the packages ship one .info.gz per distributed package. So removing the package does remove the dir entries, with no maintainer-script machinery -- which is why macaulay2.postinst contains no install-info call. The concern was real when written: dpkg triggers were new in the 2007-2008 era and before them packages ran install-info from postinst and prerm themselves. Checked against the Ubuntu PPA build of the Debian source package rather than Debian unstable

half met, half never attempted, and the check that would have caught the gap has been off since 2009. the file defers itself and the idiom would not help. Its first line is 'defer this:', its body an observation that texinfo menu items can point at a line within a node, and its last 'Maybe we can use it.' -- no problem statement, no reproducer, no acceptance criterion, and nothing in the issue tracker has ever mentioned it. M2 uses none of it: format.m2:322-328 is the only menu generator and emits '* key::' or '* key: node.', node granularity by construction, with byte offsets recorded per node at installPackage.m2:402 for the tag table alone. Nor would it pay: the form solves intra-node navigation for long prose nodes, as in the Emacs manual where one node documents dozens of hooks, whereas M2 documents one node per symbol -- 2010 nodes in a megabyte, typically 50 to 120 lines. Line references into generated output would also need line accounting threaded through the info writer and would be invalidated by every regeneration. Kept separate from 1-info-doc deliberately: that row is inter-node navigation with two closing conditions, this is intra-node with none

the need is already one call, and the file's own answer cannot work. installMethod(m,X,X,f) installs and dispatches; the asked-for installMethod((m,X,X),f) errors with 'expected method for nullary operator to be a function of 0 variables'; and the proposed fix, installMethod(Sequence,Function) := installMethod @@ append, installs cleanly -- lookup(installMethod,Sequence,Function) is non-null afterwards -- yet the call still errors, because class installMethod is CompiledFunction and a compiled function does not consult the method table. getWWW is interruptible in both phases, tested in a pty with a real ^C. Blocked in connect to 192.0.2.1, an RFC 5737 address that black-holes: ^C returns to the prompt about 4 seconds in with 'error: can't open socket : Interrupted system call', where the connect itself would run some 130 seconds. Blocked reading from a local server that accepts and never answers: ^C gives 'error: interrupted', the prompt returns and 1+1 evaluates. So the transcript in the file -- two ^C's, then the Exit (y/n) prompt and an abnormal exit -- no longer happens. The commented-out SETJMP(interrupt_jump) block at scclib.c:760-765 is still present and still marked FIXME, but it is not what makes this work: SIGINT arrives without SA_RESTART, connect returns EINTR, and the flag check surfaces it. #145, 'getWWW should time out', is open and asks for a different thing, a bound for when nobody is there to interrupt

still reproduces exactly and declined as cosmetic on the maintainer's reading. In a pty: 'i2 : f()' followed by '^Cstdio:1:16:(3):[2]: error: interrupted' on the same line, where the file asks for the message to begin on the next one and writes out both renderings to show that the line break is the whole request. Dan's transcript shows 'C-c C-c' because emacs echoes the keystroke that way; the defect is the same. The same run-on shows up in the two socket rows of this batch. No issue covers it: of nine issues with interrupt in the title six are closed, and #4144 is the adjacent live one, asking for debug info at the Exit prompt

the blocking connect is interruptible now, so the diagnosis in the file no longer holds. openInOut "$192.0.2.1:80" against a black-holed RFC 5737 address, then ^C in a pty: 'error: can't open socket : Interrupted system call' about 4 seconds in, prompt returns, 1+1 evaluates -- the system call does not continue past the handler, and the EINTR is surfaced in the message rather than swallowed. mysql is still an optional dependency (configure.ac:419) and d/mysql.d still calls mysql_real_connect, so the file's own scenario remains constructible, but the general defect it names is gone. scclib.c:760-765 still carries the commented-out SETJMP(interrupt_jump) marked FIXME; noted rather than filed, since what it would have protected works without it

the pari flags became two documented functions. the benchmark the file asks for has now been run, so the row is discharged rather than left blocked. Its precondition never arrived -- see 1-isPrime, where the pari flags became the isPrime/isPseudoprime pair -- but the comparison is still meaningful. On this machine 10^500+961 takes 10.1s for isPrime and 0.0058s for isPseudoprime, against the file's quoted 93.8s for pari's isprime(n,2) and 428.2s for Morain's ecpp; 10^800+1537 takes 70.0s and 0.019s against 508.3s and 1537s. declined on the maintainer's reading: the redesign would change documented output for every caller. the guess is right and the saving is worth having. Every List construction folds the whole list: basic.d:114-117 does r.hash = hash(r), and hash(x:List) at :82-85 is the element-by-element fold with multiplier 1299833 over the seed x.Class.hash + 23407. Cost measured: join of two 200k lists takes 11.2ms, while the identical fold over the resulting 400k elements takes 7.5-8.5ms -- measurable because a Sequence's hash is not cached, basic.d:33-36 refolding on every call -- against 0.69us to read a List's stored hash. So roughly two-thirds of join is hashing. And the fold is combinable: h(L++M) = 1299833^(#M) * (hash L - c) + hash M mod 2^64 with c = hash class L + 23407, verified on seven cases including both empty sides, mixed element types and nested lists. My first attempt used the Sequence constants seqHashSeed and seqHashMult (basic.d:8-9) and failed all five cases, which is how the two folds turned out to use different constants. The file's second half is already moot: new List from J and toSequence J on 400k elements cost 1 to 2us, because a List wraps a Sequence and they share the array. Fix site is d/actors4.d:1175-1186 plus a list() variant in basic.d taking a precomputed hash

Mike's 2008 recipe has three ingredients and they landed unevenly. Verified live with R = QQ[a,b,c,d, Degrees => {4,4,4,4}] mapping to QQ[s,t] by {s^4,s^3*t,s*t^3,t^4}, where isHomogeneous graph is true, canUseHilbertHint is true, and gb records the rawGBSetHilbertFunction log key. The recipe's last step is unmet and separately tracked -- forceGB appears 0 times in ringmap.m2, and #686 asks for exactly it, quoting the same reasoning. all three asks answered, the third against the proposal. lcm is implemented at integers.m2:64-76 -- lcm(), the ZZ and QQ pairs, the unary cases -- plus RingElement, MonomialIdeal, List and Sequence methods, and the 0-argument forms lcm {} = 1 and gcd {} = 0 arrived in PR #3328 (merged 2024-06-29). Speed: lookup(gcd,ZZ,ZZ) is a CompiledFunction, the engine's gcd0, and gcd of two roughly 700-digit integers takes 14.3us with lcm at 18.3us, since lcm(ZZ,ZZ) is abs f * (abs g // gcd(f,g)). The third ask, 'maybe not Binary method any more!', is recorded as declined rather than merely unimplemented: class gcd and class lcm are both MethodFunctionBinary, and the Binary path is the faster one -- lcm of a 2000-element list takes 9.7ms through it against 13.8ms for an explicit fold over the same list

the same gap as #4149, one character class over, so recorded there rather than as a second issue about the same function. asked and declined, on the record. the sentence is still there and still contradicts itself. Macaulay2Doc/M2-Singular-Book.m2:351 reads TEX "The following is WRONG.  In this local ring, $y$ is in the ideal $J$." followed by EXAMPLE {"y % J"}. Reproduced the whole 'Singular Book 1.4.9' node: globally y % I = y, then in QQ[x,y,z,MonomialOrder=>{Weights=>{-1,-1,-1},RevLex},Global=>false] gens gb J = matrix {{y-x*y, z-x*z}}, dim J = 1 and y % J = 0. Zero is correct -- localized at the origin x-1 is a unit, so J = (y,z) and y really is in J, which is what the sentence's own second clause says. So the manual labels a correct answer WRONG and then explains why it is right. Dan's 'wrong in a different sense' most likely points at % in a Global => false ring not being a genuine local remainder in general, which is a different claim from the printed one. both silent cases confirmed, and the asymmetry looks deliberate rather than missed. After i = "a b c", the line for i to 3 list j := i+1 warns about nothing, although the loop variable really does shield the string -- i is still "a b c" afterwards -- and the body's j := leaves j a bare Symbol outside the loop; then top-level j := 4 followed by j := 5 does warn, 'local declaration of j shields variable with same name'. the notation already works, but only for endomorphisms, which is a narrower gap than the file suggests and than I first recorded. map(R,R,{a => a^2}) on QQ[a,b] gives map(R,R,{a^2, b}), leaving b alone, because ringmap.m2:496 handles unmentioned generators when R === S and S === ring commonzero; every other case falls to :500 and errors 'destinations not specified for every generator'. So the option list is parsed either way and the sensible default exists -- it is gated on source and target being identical. The file's own example is the interesting side of that gate: for T = QQ[a] and U = T[b], the unspecified generator of map(T,U,{b => a}) is a, which is a generator of the target, so leaving it alone is well defined rather than merely convenient. Where it genuinely is not -- map(QQ[c], QQ[a,b], {a => c}) -- the present error is right. substitute takes the same spelling unconditionally since it rewrites an element rather than defining a homomorphism. Watch the positional form while changing this: map(T,U,{a}) silently expands to map(T,U,{a, a}). No issue and no pull request covers it; the search for map with destinations returns only #4578, filed from this catalog

the literal ask is unmet -- options newRing has 18 keys, all monoid options, because newring.m2:16 builds the table from applyValues(monoidDefaults, ...), and CoefficientRing is not one, so newRing(R, CoefficientRing => QQ) gives 'unknown key or option'. unmet, and low priority -- IPv6 transport works everywhere, only the literal spelling is missing. Measured against a server bound to [::1]:24602: openInOut "$ip6-localhost:24602" opens, SCSCP newConnection("ip6-localhost",24602) connects far enough to reach the handshake, getWWW "http://ip6-localhost:24602/" returns HTTP/1.0 200 OK -- and the literal form of all three errors. The resolver is already family-agnostic: scclib.c:733 sets hints.ai_family = PF_UNSPEC and opensocket passes NULL hints, so getaddrinfo returns AAAA records. The break is upstream of it, at stdio.d:227-231, which splits $host:service on the FIRST colon and breaks; for $::1:24601 host0 comes out empty, and stdio.d:233 reads an empty host as 'listener', so a connect attempt silently becomes a bind attempt with service ":1:24601". Three colon-splitters exist and only one is right: SCSCP/client.m2:79 uses greedy ^(.*)\:(.*)$, i.e. the last colon, which is correct for IPv6, then re-concatenates at :23 and openInOut undoes it; splitWWW errors on http://[::1]:24602/. Filing only the stdio.d half. The argument is the documented idiom rather than IPv6 adoption: every socket example in the tree is an IPv4 literal (newConnection("127.0.0.1",26135), startServer "127.0.0.1", the SCSCP docinput transcripts, #4527's bind-loopback advice) and none has an IPv6 spelling. the mismatch is gone. The error was that poincare Ideal computed the series of the quotient -- 'poincare ((ring I)^1/I)' -- while module Ideal copied I.cache.poincare onto image generators I, the submodule, whose series is different. Today poincare Ideal := I -> poincare comodule I (hilbert.m2:81) with comodule Ideal := I -> cokernel generators I (matrix1.m2:438), and module Ideal := (cacheValue symbol module)(I -> image generators I) (matrix1.m2:440) has the poincare-copying line deleted. Measured over QQ[x,y] with I = ideal(x^2,x*y): poincare I is 1-2*T^2+T^3, poincare module I is 2*T^2-T^3, and they sum to 1 as they must; module I does not inherit the ideal's value. Checked the MonomialIdeal path too, since poincare MonomialIdeal does cache under I.cache.poincare (monideal.m2:131): for monomialIdeal(x^2,x*y) that value is 1-2*T^2+T^3, the quotient's series, and module J still comes back with no cached poincare -- so there is nothing left to copy onto the wrong module

unmet as asked, and not worth the cost: the checks would run uname and a directory test in every login shell to defend against a shared home directory spanning architectures, which is Dan's 2006 scenario (his transcript checks uname -m/-s/-r/-p on rhodium) and is rare now. setup() is otherwise unchanged in shape: it writes ~/.profile-Macaulay2 and inserts a loader into ~/.bash_profile, ~/.bash_login, ~/.profile or ~/.zprofile (files.m2:499-508), hard-coding the prefix into PATH, MANPATH, INFOPATH and LD_LIBRARY_PATH (:439-443), and the bash template's only logic is avoiding a duplicate entry (:410-418) -- nothing tests that the directory still exists or which machine it is on. It is user-facing and documented (setup-doc.m2), recommended for installs outside a standard location. One caveat worth keeping if this is revisited: three of the four variables are inert when stale, but LD_LIBRARY_PATH reaches every dynamically linked program in the login session, so a wrong-architecture entry there is the only part with consequences beyond M2. setup() has real history in the tracker, all about which shell to munge -- #1061/#1067, #1138, #1139, #1405/#1406, #1460, all closed -- and #1068 is open, 'setup() should examine $SHELL'; nothing about validating the prefix or the architecture

maintainer's call: a pruned ring is a different ring, and giving the eliminated symbols values in it -- even optionally -- trades a clear error for cross-ring confusion of the kind #666 and 0-synonyms-and-collisions are about. Unmet as asked, and the state is worth recording. use assigns only gens Rp, so for R = QQ[a,b,c]/(a-b-1) and Rp = minimalPresentation R = QQ[b..c], after use Rp we have ring a = R and ring b = Rp, and both a+b and a*b error. The ingredient the ask needs does exist: R.minimalPresentationMap is map(Rp,R,{b+1,b,c}), sending a to b+1 in Rp, so an implementation would not have to compute anything. One trap for anyone who revisits it: map(Rp,R) looks like the same map and returns b+1 for a, but only because a's normal form in R is already b+1, so it agrees by accident rather than by recording the correspondence. Nothing in the tracker matches prune, pruningMap, minimalPresentationMap, use Ring or eliminated variable

the suggestion was tested and the code declines it. pushForward1 is gone -- changes.m2:1827 records "'pushForward1(f,M)' has been replaced by 'relations coimage map(M,f)'" and the only survivals are commented-out doc at pushForward-doc.m2:95-121 -- and tu_canEmbed.m2:254-256 now reads ff1 = map(R,S,can1); G = map(coker F1,ff1); trim coimage G, giving betti {(0,{0},0)=>1, (1,{2},2)=>10}. Substituting the surviving function, pushForward(ff1, coker F1), errors 'no applicable strategy for computing pushforward' (pushforward.m2:103), and the reason is mathematical rather than a missing case: the Default strategy needs a homogeneous map and M/ideal f.matrix finite-dimensional, and here isHomogeneous ff1 is false and dim(M/ideal ff1.matrix) is 1; the Quotient strategy (Justin Chen, from #1522) needs a common ambient ring with source among target.baseRings, and neither holds. ff1 is a rational map P2 --> P6 by cubics through three points, so it is not module-finite and coimage, which computes the ideal of the image, is the right tool. PR search done rather than issue search only, since pushForward is under active development: Joel Dodge's #4366 (merged, towers and differing coefficient rings), #4435 (open, relaxes a degree-map restriction, failing example errors 'unexpected degree map of ring map' inside pushNonLinear) and #4465 (queued behind it). All widen which finite maps are accepted, which is a different axis from this row -- this map fails the homogeneity gate first. One wording gap left unfiled: the prose still says 'compute its push-forward under the map' while the code says coimage, and Dan hyphenated push-forward in the same 2008 diff, apparently so it would not read as a function name

not an M2 bug: a scratch C file exploring whether Python can be embedded in a C program, quoting William Stein on making Sage's 'from sage.all import *' avoid importing IPython so that 'sage -python' and 'sage -c' start faster. three asks: the third is met, the first two are one thing and are measured. Ask 3, an example of a dynamically loaded C library in a python module, is done well beyond the request -- installNumPyMethods with worked examples in Python/doc/numpy.m2 converting M2 matrices and vectors to NumPy arrays, plus a matplotlib tutorial with a rendered twisted-cubic.png; both are C extension modules in M2's embedded CPython. Asks 1 and 2 unmet: python.d:28 builds pythonObjectCell(po, hash_t(0)) with no registerFinalizer and no Py_DECREF, and the only three Py_DECREF calls in the interface (python-c.c:163,175,219) are on conversion temporaries. Measured two ways: sys.getrefcount on a list held in __main__ goes 2 -> 3 when M2 wraps it and stays 3 after the M2 reference is dropped and collectGarbage() and gc.collect() are both run; and 20 objects created in a loop with no M2 reference kept are all still alive afterwards. Caveat on the proof, since only the two together are conclusive: a refcount that stays put is also consistent with Boehm not having collected the cell, and that cannot be distinguished by observation precisely because there is no finalizer to watch fire. registerFinalizer exists as a MethodFunction, so the mechanism is available; the work is deciding per toExpr call site whether the reference is owned or borrowed, a wrong DECREF being worse than the leak, which is presumably why Dan wrote it as a task. Correcting an earlier claim of mine: Python.m2 has 14 TEST blocks, so the package is tested -- what is true is that none touches refcounts, lifetime or GC, and the three-line check above would be one. Searched issues and PRs: the interface has had a lot of work (#2130, #2302, #2316, #2523, #2605, #2631, #2639, #2692, #3025) and none is about reference counting

the same defect as #4515, which this catalog filed four days ago from 0-quotient-for-non-free-modules, and which leads with the well-definedness claim. Reproduces exactly, with an asymmetry #4515's example does not have: for f = inducedMap(R^1/x, R^1/x^2) and g = inducedMap(R^1/x, R^1/x^3) over ZZ/101[x], quotientRemainder(g,f) has isWellDefined first true while quotientRemainder(f,g) has it false. The mathematics agrees, which is why it is a good test case: quotientRemainder(f,g) wants q : R^1/x^2 -> R^1/x^3, and 1 sends x^2 to x^2, nonzero in R/x^3, whereas the other direction sends x^3 to 0 in R/x^2. Commented on #4515 with the pair and Dan's 2006 email asking 'Did I just not think about whether the resulting maps are well-defined?'

does not reproduce, with the caveat that the file says the corruption happened only 'sometimes!'. Ran Anton's transcript five times -- M2 as 'openInOut openListener "$:PORT"', a python client sending 'hi there', a 60-character buffer string held across the read -- and the buffer was byte-identical afterwards every time; the file's diagnostic, substring(buffer,0,#newstring) == newstring, is false, where in the bug it was true because the read had overwritten the buffer's head. duplicate of #708 'floating point weirdness', open since 2017 and worked on by the maintainer, whose own body closes with toExternalString oo -> .9007199254740991p53e16, the same function this file shows. State today: the transcript's trailing e0 is gone (toExternalString .3 is .29999999999999999p53) and the value round-trips, but seventeen significant digits are emitted where one would do, since value ".3p53" == .3. Not a blanket policy -- .5 and .25 print as .5p53 and .25p53 because those decimals are exact in binary, and 1. prints .1p53e1 -- so M2 prints short when it can be exact and otherwise falls back to full precision. The maintainer's comment of 2024-11-03 states the mechanism and the obstacle: 'using mpfr_get_str, we get the mathematically closest option. But for readability, we probably want the option with the fewest number of digits. There are various algorithms for this (Dragon4, Grisu3, Ryu), but as far as I can tell, they haven't been implemented for MPFR yet.' #3477 bumped p53 digits from 15 to 16 and that comment notes 17 is required, which matches the 17 measured here; #1579 is collateral. Commented with the one thing the row adds, that the symptom shows on an ordinary number rather than only near 2^53. Search note: the cache found nothing because the decisive text is in a comment and bin/fetch-issues does not cache comments, and #708's title shares no vocabulary with this row -- gh search issues, which does index comments, found it on the term 'ryu'
