the file asks 'What does this code do?' and adds 'If it's not important, get rid of it', so the conditional is what decides it, and the answer is that it is important. Option ++ Option := directSum at matrix.m2:368 with Option.directSum below is the labelled-direct-summand machinery, and it is documented: directSum-doc.m2:75-112 lists (symbol++, Option, Option) among its keys, says the preferred indices 'can be specified with code like directSum(a=>M,b=>N,...)', adds 'Similar syntax works with ++', and gives F = (a => ZZ^1) ++ (b => ZZ^2) as the example. Verified: directSum(a => M, b => N) gives R^3, Q_[a] gives the inclusion, indices Q gives {a, b}, components Q gives {R^1, R^2}. (a => 1) ++ (b => 2) errors with 'no method for direct sum of integers', which is honest -- there is no direct sum of integers. Recorded for the record since it puzzled the file's author: ++ means merge on OptionTable (option.m2:48-49, merge(opts1,opts2,last)) and direct sum on Option, and the reason is age -- Option ++ Option := directSum dates from b4f69c9270 (1998-06-24), nine years before OptionTable ++ OptionTable arrived in f1c1dd78f1 (2007-12-23), so they never collided. No comment at matrix.m2:368 says what it is for, which is why the question arose; the answer lives only in the documentation

Obsolete: # File is gone, lookup(symbol #, File) returning null, which is what the entry proposed; and Module ~, Ideal ~ and Ring ~ no longer exist at all, sheafification being spelled sheaf now. Answered rather than fixed: Option ++ Option resolves to directSum, which is labelled direct sums, so the entry's 'what is that?' has a sensible answer; and WrapperType is documented at doc12.m2:21. Moved out of scope: CoherentSheaf ZZ now lives at packages/Varieties.m2:366, so it is Varieties' documentation to write. Filed: ask 7, that Ideal ? Ideal is undefined so sort fails on a list of ideals while the module analogue exists precisely to permit sorting; and ask 8, which per Doug's instruction gathers all fourteen 'modernize this node' entries into a single issue rather than filing them one by one -- asks 2, 6, 8, 10, 13, 14, 17, 18, 21, 27, 29, 31, 32 and 33 all carry its number. Three mistakes of mine are worth recording. First, I surveyed the doc sources by splitting on 'document {' only, which hid all 17 doc/// nodes in these files and made and/or/not look unmet; the same bug produced a false positive, reporting examples on symbol ^** that actually belonged to the doc/// block following it. Second, I built the consolidated issue on the premise that roughly fifty nodes wrongly lack Usage, before finding that a bare-symbol node carrying only a Headline is the deliberate convention -- those are overview pages with Subnodes and SeeAlso -- so the issue was narrowed to nodes missing a Headline outright, siblings that diverged within one file, and nodes where only a headline was ever written. Third, I described the ? gap as '? Ideal' when that is the unary method, which works; Doug pointed out that the binary Ideal ? Ideal is the distinct thing that is missing. Also corrected in passing: I read Module ? Module as a containment comparison when its own source comment says 'used for sorting a list of modules' and it compares rank then degrees, which is what makes the == node's caveat about ? correct -- verified by image matrix{{x}} and image matrix{{y}} being ==-false but ?-equal.

a prediction, marked 'urgency: low', and it did not come true. The file says 'inheritance via lookup will probably stop working if any immutable types are involved, installing a method might go to one of the immutable types'. Built the chain it worries about -- zzI = new ImmutableType of HashTable, zzY = new Type of zzI, a method installed on zzY -- and lookup from an instance finds it: zzz + zzz returns 'from Y', with ancestors zzY giving {zzY, ImmutableType{}, HashTable, Thing}, so the immutable ancestor is traversed without trouble. The second clause is what immutability is for, and it fails rather than corrupting anything: (zzI + zzI) := ... errors. reproduces verbatim and is taste rather than defect. Built the node the file quotes -- Outputs => { List => "of global symbols matching the pattern" } -- and help renders '* a "list", of global symbols matching the pattern', the same comma the file objects to, twenty years on. The comma is doing work: it separates the type from the description, and without it 'a list of global symbols' gives the reader no way to see where the type ends. The idiom, a bare type key with a continuation phrase, is used throughout Macaulay2Doc, so changing the rendering would churn a great many pages for a punctuation preference. A judgment, and cheap to overrule by anyone with a view on the typography

'any string used as a key in a ring is a assumed to harbor a generator of the ring, so caching things there is a bad idea' -- the two namespaces are separate now, so caching there is safe. both forms now give the same answer, and it is the right one -- but the file marks the wrong line as the bug. In toField(QQ[x]/(x^2+1)), x is a unit: x^(-1) = -x and x*(-x) = 1, so ideal(x) is the unit ideal and 1 % ideal(x) must be 0. The file records 1 % ideal(x) = 1 without comment and annotates 1 % x = 0 as 'wrong answer', which is backwards -- 0 was always correct and 1 was the wrong one. Today both give 0, and ideal(x) == ideal 1_F confirms why. J. Yu's report and Mike's own diagnosis point at the right place regardless: Number % Ideal calls gb(I, DegreeLimit=>0) when the ideal is homogeneous, and the note reads 'the problem is that gb stops at degree limit 0 but perhaps that has a different meaning in the engine than at top level'

its closing ask, 'one of these operations should say something about finding a zero divisor!!', is met over multivariate quotients and unmet over univariate ones, which is what the issue reports. In toField(ZZ/101[u]/(u^2-1)), 1/(u-1) raises the engine's generic 'either element not invertible, or no method available to compute its inverse' from Ring::power (ring.cpp:127-139) and getNonUnit returns null; add one unused variable, toField(ZZ/101[p,q]/(p^2-1)), and the same division raises 'a non unit was found in a ring declared to be a field' with getNonUnit giving p-1. Same split for QQ[s]/(s^2-1) against ZZ/101[w,z]/(w*z), so it tracks variable count rather than coefficient ring or shape of relation. The good path runs through Ring::set_non_unit (ring.cpp:88-95), the tail of the machinery 4cbb7fef7d fixed for #1895; the univariate path never reaches it. Everything else in the file has resolved: block 1 over the genuine field ZZ/101[a]/(a^2+a+1) passes all six assertions, and both assertions marked '-- still failing' in block 2 ask for the wrong thing -- 1//(1-a) = 0 is correct division with remainder since 1%(1-a) = 1 and 0*(1-a)+1 = 1, and 1/(a-1) fails its equality test because it raises, which it should, a-1 being a zero divisor

the question it asks -- of b^2 = 0 for a degree-2 skew variable, 'is this really what we intend?' -- is still open, and the documentation answers it the other way. The 'exterior algebras' node states xy = (-1)^(deg x deg y) yx with 'if deg(x) is odd, then x^2 = 0' as a consequence, degrees taken from the ring. The implementation ignores degrees entirely: on the doc page's own example ring QQ[a,b,r,s,t, SkewCommutative=>true, Degrees=>{2,2,1,1,1}], r*a == a*r is false where the rule gives +1, a*b == b*a is false for two even-degree variables, and a*a is 0 though even degree does not force it. The two agree exactly when all degrees are 1, which is the default and every other example on the page. Filed without picking a side, as the user directed: both readings are defensible and the rule is not a recent slip -- PR #4252 (2026-05-03) only restyled the node, changing one file and no code, and the sentence it replaced said the same thing back to e4d91062d9, 2001-05-18, by the author of this bugs file. Checked 23 candidates from sixteen search terms; the nearest, #3123, is about towers rather than degrees

eight observations, one still concrete and live: graphIdeal and graphRing declare MonomialOrder among their options and silently discard it, which is this file's own 'doesn't make use of options'. MonomialOrder => Lex and MonomialOrder => {Weights => {5,1,1}} both give output identical to the default, while tensor -- which graphIdeal calls -- honours the same option and gives Lex => 3. Cause is newring.m2:113-117, where opts is passed to tensor and MonomialOrder => Eliminate m follows it and wins; not a straight reordering, since the elimination order is the point of the function. The result is also cached under the ignored options, at newring.m2:97. VariableBaseName and MonomialSize both work. Of the rest: pushNonLinear no longer exists, so 'not documented even in the code' is moot; 'fraction fields of tower poly rings should work!!' now do, frac(QQ[a][b]) being a field with (b/a)*(a/b) == 1; basis has since gained a SourceRing option, plausibly the 'RingMap option' asked for. the question it asks, 'Is the sign right?', is no, and the cause is that no normalization is applied at all. Elimination.m2:128 is discriminant(f,x) = resultant(f, diff(x,f), x), where the standard discriminant is (-1)^(n(n-1)/2) times that divided by the leading coefficient. Both omissions show: discriminant(x^2+b*x+c, x) gives -b^2+4c against the familiar b^2-4c, and discriminant(a*x^2+b*x+c, x) gives -a*b^2+4*a^2*c, which is -a times b^2-4ac. The sign follows the exponent exactly rather than being a blanket flip, which is what identifies the missing factor: against the product-of-differences formula, degree 2 and degree 3 come out negated, exponents 1 and 3, while degree 4 agrees, exponent 6. The documentation states no convention -- the Outputs clause reads only 'the discriminant of f with respect to x' -- and the example on the node is a quadratic, so the rendered page shows the flipped value with nothing to explain it. Filed with both resolutions stated and neither recommended, at the user's direction: documenting the convention breaks nothing, normalizing the output changes results for every existing caller. Labelled under discussion for that reason. Not #4449, which is discriminant raising 'expected nonzero polynomials' when the derivative vanishes identically in characteristic p. Duplicate search redone after being asked whether I had done it: 12 candidates from 'discriminant' plus 'resultant' narrowed by sign/convention wording, read #38 (resultant wrong for a degree-0 argument, closed) and #4449. PR #4472 is open against #4449 and rewrites this same line, adding an early return when the derivative vanishes; it leaves the normalization alone, so the two are independent but adjacent, and the issue says so

the extra constant is still there, it is a genuine generator rather than a printing artifact, and the resulting object is not an ideal. Over R = (QQ[w]/(w^4+w^3+w^2+w+1))[x,y] the file reports newMonomialIdeal(R, rawMonomialIdeal(raw matrix {{x}}, 0)) coming back as monomialIdeal(x, -w^3-w^2-w-1) and calls the constant wrong. Distinct from #4625, filed earlier today from 0-rawAlexanderDual, whose ring has no quotient in the coefficient ring and whose generator count is right, the failure there being in dual. no leak, by the rising-n method rather than the single measurement the file uses. Its annotations rank the variants -- search0 'doesn't go up much', search1 'doesn't go up', search2 'did go up', search3 'up to 244 M (227 M with MonomialSize=>8)', search4 '177 M' -- so search3 is the worst case. Running its core, pickAssemble on the 4-revolute setup over ZZ/5 followed by (dim I, degree I), at rising n in one process: 3678210 bytes per call at n=50 as the heap grows from 125 to 305 MB, then 40.96, 20.48 and 20.48 bytes per call at n = 100, 200 and 400, with resident memory pinned at 304.6 MB and 16 kB of total growth across the last 700 calls. two engine-level suggestions for Schubert2, both still unimplemented, filed at the user's direction over my recommendation to park them. fractions are not reduced when the base ring has relations, and the file is named for the consequence. Over frac(QQ[x]/(x^5-2)[y]), (x/(y-2)+1+x*y)^4 has denominator with leading coefficient 1443087550851217253118659088405235200, 37 digits; the file's own recorded session shows the same, with numbers like 438345528176005822616124236928000. The factor is exactly removable -- writing C for it, denominator == C*(y-2)^4 is true, C divides the numerator, and dividing out leaves coefficients of one or two digits -- and the same shape over frac(QQ[z]) reduces properly to z^4-8z^3+24z^2-32z+16. Cause is frac.cpp:38-46: the FractionField constructor clears use_gcd_simplify whenever the base ring is a quotient, so the branch holding divide_by_given_content never runs; two lines below sits an acknowledged '#warning frac simplify: doesn't handle towers of fracs'. Probably downstream of #4622, gcd being unavailable over such rings. The user asked whether PR #4462 fixes it: on reading its diff, no -- it adds simplify_unit_denominator, which returns early for a non-unit denominator like C*(y-2)^4, leaving the same disabled branch -- but that branch was not built, so the issue records this as a reading rather than a measurement

the demo no longer demonstrates anything, measured against libgc 8.2.6. The file is a 46-line C program, not M2 code, whose header says it 'demonstrates that gc has trouble with interior pointers, and that early garbage collection at fortuitous times ... can help', and whose trailing comment gives the recipe: build plain, with -DMASK=0xff, and with -DCOLLECTOFTEN, each under ulimit -v 400000, the premise being that the plain build blows past 400 MB while the eagerly-collecting one survives. Built all three and sampled RSS every 2 s for 20 s: all three sit flat at 2 MB and none grows. GC_PRINT_STATS explains why -- the plain build already performs about 19,000 complete collections in 10 s unprompted, and COLLECTOFTEN merely doubles that to about 41,000, so the collector reclaims this allocation pattern without being asked. Independently, the recipe could not be used as written today: ulimit -v caps address space, not resident memory, and libgc reserves far more address space than it touches, so the limit kills the process at startup instead of measuring its heap. GC_all_interior_pointers, the switch the whole demo turns on, is now deprecated and warns at compile time

the file's one example reproduces verbatim, twenty years on, and the general complaint it opens with -- 'a routine is called, it returns an illegitimate value, and the caller interprets it as a particular type of error' -- turns out to describe the exact code that two other rows in this batch also land on. Running the Schubert2 block and then (alarm 3; f^-1) gives 'error: either element not invertible, or no method available to compute its inverse', three runs out of three; the wording has changed since 2006 but not the content. The control matters here because f could simply be a non-unit: with the alarm removed, f^-1 was still running after 2 minutes, so the alarm is what ends it and the message is about the wrong thing. Mechanism: Ring::power (rings/ring.cpp:127-139) handles a negative exponent by calling invert and then testing is_zero on the result as its failure sentinel, so any path that abandons invert mid-computation -- an interrupt among them -- yields zero and gets reported as a domain error, overwriting the interrupt. Evidence the interrupt is still known at that point: wrapping the same expression in try reports 'alarm occurred' instead, which is the other bug, #3371 (try fails to catch alarm), and not this one -- do not conflate them. Nothing tracks this: #1392 is alarms dropped entirely, #168 interrupts not arriving, #4144 and #4567 unrelated. Distinct from bugs/dan/0-interrupts, parked as a research question about the d language. Filing on the concrete example rather than on the audit the file asks for.

the file is Mike's working notes on tuning the reducer-selection heuristic for local Groebner bases, not a defect report, and its annotations describe the heuristic rather than accusing M2. Read the parenthetical: 'S_2 % gb1; -- this one is bad, at least for this choice (min alpha, min size)' names the strategy being evaluated. Measured it anyway, because the surface reading is alarming. Over kk = ZZ/101 in kk[t,x,y,z, MonomialOrder => Weights => 4:-1, Global => false], the harder example's full basis is 7 elements in 8 ms and 13 lead-term syzygies come back instantly; reducing them one M2 process each under timeout 90 gives 9 of 13 in under a millisecond and 4 over 90 s, and the four are exactly S_2, S_5, S_8, S_11, the four the file marks. The minimal case, f = -t^7*G_1 + y^5*G_2 = 12*t^10*y*z-3*t^8*y^2*z^2+9*t^8*y*z^3+18*t^9*y*z^3-t^7*x^8-32*t^3*x^2*y^6*z^4-32*t^2*x*y^8*z^7, exceeds 1500 s. None of that is a bug, and gbTrace 15 says why: in 60 s it takes 17,639 reduction steps, every intermediate distinct so there is no cycle, the intermediate grows monotonically from 7 terms to 6,951, and Mora's own measure descends -- h_alpha goes 6, 5, ... 2 while the chosen reducer is always t*z at ecart 2 rather than t^7 at ecart 6, which is the correct minimum-ecart choice. So the algorithm makes legal monotone progress throughout and this is intermediate expression swell: the reducer t*z+4*t^2*z+3*z^3+6*t*z^3 has a tail of higher degree than its lead term, so every cancellation against it adds terms, and the slow four are the syzygies whose lead terms force repeated reduction by it. Two traps worth recording. Flat RSS at ~300 MB looks like a cycle and is not -- 7,000 terms is a few hundred KB, so memory cannot see this swell; and neither input size nor ecart predicts the slow four (S_11 is the largest at 133 terms and slow, S_12 at 121 is fast; S_8 has the lowest ecart of all thirteen and is slow), so ruling those out is not evidence of a defect either. In-process timing is also unusable here: alarm does not interrupt the engine's reduction, so try (alarm 60; f % gb1) ran past 79 s, which is the #1392 and #3371 family -- use one process per case under an external timeout. Same conclusion the sibling 1-gb-local-bugs.m2 reached for its non-termination cases. the SIGSEGV Moty Katzman reported in 0.9.95 is long gone -- the file records that itself, '10/26/08: now get an error message on y/(u^2+v^2)' -- and the error message it was downgraded to is #3449, open since 2024-09 with the same one-line shape: in R = frac(QQ[x,y])[z], 1/x_R raises 'not implemented yet: fraction fields of polynomial rings over rings other than ZZ, QQ, or a finite field' while x_R^-1 returns 1/x. Confirmed the two are one defect and not merely one message: in the file's own K = frac(ZZ/5[u,v]), R = K[x,y,z_0..z_9], u^2+v^2 already lies in K, and ((u^2+v^2)_R)^-1 gives 1/(u^2+v^2) and y*(1/(u^2+v^2)) gives (1/(u^2+v^2))*y, both in R, while y/(u^2+v^2) raises. The cause is that RingElement / RingElement (enginering.m2:690-705) promotes the coefficient into R and then, with both sides in one ring, calls frac R, which is what is unimplemented -- so the divisor being a unit of the coefficient field never gets used. RingElement / Number sidesteps it by computing (1/g)*f, which is why y/2 stays in R. #3449 is the row's issue; nothing to file.

the routine asked for does not exist and the need it was for is not there to be met. Dan wanted 'a raw multiplication routine that would multiply two polynomials f and g discarding the terms of weight >= n wrt a weight vector v', to speed up power series expansion 'by a factor of 2 or 1.333'. Still absent: sweeping every raw name under Macaulay2/d for mult, part, weight or trunc gives rawGetPart and rawGetParts, which extract from a product already formed, rawWeightRange, and the dense-matrix rawLinAlg*Mult -- none takes a cutoff. And the multiply-then-discard pattern is still in Core, at hilbert.m2:12-26 where recipN iterates g = g + tr(g * (1 - tr(g * tr f))) with tr = h -> part(, m-1, wts, h), and at hilbert.m2:30 in truncatePower. So the ask is unmet in the strict sense. Measured whether it matters, and it does not. The only consumer is truncateSeries (hilbert.m2:33-42), reached only from hilbertSeries(M, Order => n) with n finite (hilbert.m2:336 and 362). Note what it feeds recipN: pow#0 of Product{Power{1 - T_i, e}}, i.e. a *binomial* -- for QQ[x_0..x_5] the denominator is (1-T)^6 and recipN inverts 1-T. Instrumented copies of recipN and truncatePower on exactly those inputs discard 31-44% of the terms formed, flat in the order (6 vars Order 50: 353 formed, 239 kept, 32%; 6 vars Order 200: 31%; 10 vars Order 200: 38%; 20 vars Order 100 and Order 400: 44% both), so Dan's factor of 2 was slightly optimistic but the right order of magnitude as a term-count ratio. The trouble is what it is a fraction of: end to end on fresh modules, so nothing comes from M.cache#approxKey, hilbertSeries(M, Order => n) costs 0.003 s at 6 vars Order 50, 0.033 s at 6 vars Order 200, 0.095 s at 10 vars Order 200 and 0.20 s at 20 vars Order 100. Saving 40% of that is 0.08 s, and 40% of the terms is a ceiling rather than a saving, because a truncating multiply must still test each candidate term's weight against the cutoff -- it trades term construction for a comparison. Two limits on the measurement, so a maintainer can weigh it: term count is a proxy for multiplication cost rather than a timing, and I instrumented top-level copies of the two routines rather than profiling Core itself. A first attempt measured the wrong thing entirely, feeding recipN product(nv, i -> 1 - T_i), which nothing in Core does; the input is always a binomial, which is why there is so little to throw away. Reverse this if a consumer appears that inverts a dense multivariate series -- the shape of the win depends entirely on that, not on the routine.

reproduces, and it is the zero-ring corner of #3973 rather than its own defect: both are x^-1 failing when it should not, on Ring::power's negative-exponent path (rings/ring.cpp:127-139). #3973 is r^-1 in a toField tower aborting with 'ring element gcd computation failed'; this one is R = QQ[x]/1 where x^-1 raises 'either element not invertible, or no method available to compute its inverse'. The two faults differ in where they land -- #3973 dies inside invert, this misreads what invert returned -- so the shared entry point is what makes them one row rather than two, and the zero-ring case belongs on that thread as an additional demonstration. The contradiction is sharper than the file's transcript: in the zero ring isUnit x is true, x*(1//x) == 1 is true, x^0 is 0, and inverse matrix{{x}} correctly returns the zero matrix, so four separate parts of M2 agree x is a unit and only RingElement ^ ZZ refuses; even 1_R^-1 fails, i.e. the ring cannot invert its own identity. The zero ring is right to call x a unit, since 1 = 0 there and so 0*0 = 0 = 1, and the inverse being withheld is 0. Cause: Ring::power tests is_zero on invert's result as its failure sentinel, which cannot distinguish a correct zero inverse from a failed one. That sentinel arrived in d97f303f2d, the commit that settles the sibling row 1-inverses, so the two rows are two sides of one 2006 change; and the same line is what mis-describes an interrupt in 1-interrupts. It is not only pathological input: QQ[x,y]/ideal(x, 1+x) is the zero ring with nobody having written 1, which is the shape any quotient takes when the ideal turns out to be everything. Same in ZZ/1 and ZZ/5[]/1, so it tracks the zero ring rather than the presentation. The two issues where this sentinel misfired the other way are both genuinely fixed, checked: #1314, where t^-1 in QQ[t]/t^3 returned 1, and #2208's inverse of 0 over ZZ/5 now both raise. Searched titles and bodies for invertible, inverse, unit, isUnit, negative power, zero ring, trivial ring, and comments via gh search for Ring::power, is_zero, invert, not invertible and noninvertible; #97 and #1519 are the only near titles and neither is about inversion.

the crash the file is named for is gone, and what remains is the cost of asking for much more than the file needed. Sonja Petrovic's script ends at intersect(Itree1deg3, Itree2deg3) over a 256-variable ring, two ideals of 64 cubics each from the 3-minors of four 4x4 matrices; the file records 'ran out of memory!!' and then '---in Macaulay2.1.1, Dec.08, I get a bus error.' Dan's question is 'pushForward1 has been supplanted by coimage, but pushForward1 had many options, no longer available. Is that a problem?' and the answer is mostly no, with one gap that is filable. Of the eight options he lists, DegreeLimit and Strategy are on kernel by name, BasisElementLimit's analogue for an elimination is SubringLimit, and UseHilbertFunction is better than restored -- the AffineRing strategy calls canUseHilbertHint itself and then asserts the hint was used, so it is automatic rather than the caller's decision. MonomialOrder, PairLimit, StopBeforeComputation and StopWithMinimalGenerators have no successor. Note that pushForward is not the successor and is the wrong comparison: it requires the map to be module-finite, which pushForward1 never did, and on the rational normal curve map it raises 'no applicable strategy for computing pushforward'. coimage is, via changes.m2:1827, 'pushForward1(f,M) has been replaced by relations coimage map(M,f)'. The gap: coimage RingMap is one expression, f.source / kernel f at ringmap.m2:375, declared with no option table, and isInjective RingMap at :377 is the same shape, so neither can pass kernel's options through -- coimage(F, SubringLimit => 1) and isInjective(F, SubringLimit => 1) both raise 'no method found', and options coimage and options isInjective are both null. There is no image RingMap, so those two are the whole affected set. kernel's options do work, which took a control to establish: kernel RingMap caches on the map and the underlying gb caches on the graph matrix, so re-testing variants against one F in one session shows them apparently ignored. With a fresh ring and map per variant, over R = ZZ/101[a..d] and S = ZZ/101[s,t] with F = map(S,R,{s^4,s^3*t,s*t^3,t^4}), no options gives 4 generators of degrees {2,3,3,3}, SubringLimit => 1 gives 1, SubringLimit => 2 gives 2 and DegreeLimit => 2 gives 0. Searched titles and bodies for coimage, pushForward, pushForward1, kernel, SubringLimit, and comments via gh search for pushForward1, coimage and minPres, PRs included: nothing covers it. #3284 is the nearest open neighbour, kernel misbehaving under pushFwd on multigraded input, which is about answers rather than options; #4366, #4435, #4465 and #4176 are all widening which ring maps pushForward accepts, a different axis. Sibling row bugs/dan/1-pushForward1 is settled wontfix on a different ask -- whether a tutorial's suggestion to use pushForward1 still works.

a working scratch file on radical algorithms, not a defect report, and its one real assertion passes. Over R = ZZ/101[a..i] with M = genericMatrix(R,a,3,3) and I = ideal(M^3), radical I is ideal(trace M, trace M^2, trace M^3) exactly as the file asserts, in 2.87 s; the file's own line radical(I, CompleteIntersection=>I1) cannot run as written because I1 is never defined anywhere in it, but with the trace ideal supplied it returns in 0.00007 s, which is what that option is for -- the radical here is a codimension-3 complete intersection. Of the two things the file marks '-- not good', one is fixed and one is not, and the difference is which machinery they use. decompose I now takes 2.9 s, because radical's default moved onto the Groebner route in 74d4d90749, the same change that settles the sibling row 1-radical.m2. top I still exhausts a 4 GB cap after about ten minutes, and so do associatedPrimes I and Ext^2 and Ext^3 of R/I, while res R^1/I takes 0.10 s with betti {1,9,36,85,128,127,84,36,9,1}. So the split is Ext-based against Groebner-based, and topComponents Ideal is annihilator Ext^codim(R/I,R) with no alternative strategy. This is scale rather than a defect, on three pieces of evidence. The same construction one size down is instant across the board -- for the 2x2 nilpotent ideal in ZZ/101[p,q,r,s], also depth 0 and also not unmixed, Ext^2 takes 0.0023 s, top 0.013 s, associatedPrimes 0.16 s and radical 0.036 s -- so the code path is sound. There is no discontinuity at the codimension: Ext^1 of the 3x3 module takes 0.115 s and Ext^2 is already past 84 s and 1.9 GB, so the cost grows steadily rather than jumping where topComponents happens to look. And the module is the worst case for Ext methods by construction: the resolution has ten terms, so pdim R^1/I is 9 over nine variables and depth is 0 by Auslander-Buchsbaum, which means the origin is an associated prime, I is not unmixed, top I is genuinely not I, and Ext^i(R/I,R) is nonzero all the way to i = 9. What is missing is a route to top that is not Ext, which is a capability gap rather than a bug; #293, standard bases for local rings, is the nearest thing to a wishlist entry for that class. Searched titles and bodies for topComponents, removeLowestDimension, annihilator, dimensional, and comments via gh search for topComponents, remove_low_dim and annihilator Ext; 'top' alone is useless as a term, returning thirty hits of 'topic' and 'top-level'. Three open neighbours, none of them this: #622 is topComponents giving the wrong answer in a quotient ring, #4308 says topComponents Module is broken via saturate but this row exercises topComponents Ideal, which never calls saturate, and #4278 is the Complexes resolution slowdown, ruled out because OldChainComplexes' Ext^3 on this input is equally slow -- fourteen minutes with no result.

the question the file asks in its first line, 'Do resolutions still have memory leaks? 1 May 2009', answers no on both of its halves. the one computation the file could not finish now finishes in about twenty minutes. Its complaint is a single comment: 'to check the guess, we try to compute the regularity of the Rees algebra, but this seems to be too hard: M2 spent 3 days and 2.5 GB of memory trying before I ran low on memory and killed the process.' Today reesIdeal(L, L_0) takes 12.4 s and gives 79 generators, and res of the flattened ideal takes 1190 s -- measured three times at 1191, 1206 and 1190 s -- so the betti table the file was after is now obtainable. Everything before that complaint is fast and matches what the file says: the Horrocks-Mumford bundle presents in 0.008 s via BGG's beilinson, regularity FHM is 5, res coker mapcone is 0.016 s, and IX comes out as 18 generators, 3 of degree 5 and 15 of degree 6 -- the file's 'the ideal of the abelian surface: 3 quintics and 15 sextics' -- of codimension 2 and degree 10. Getting the file's actual target needed care in two places. The weight vector {1,1,1,1,0,0,0,0,0} has nine entries and ring IRX reports four, because the Rees ideal sits in a tower; it is the flattened ring that has nine, ordered {w_0..w_3, x_0..x_4}, so the 1s land on the Rees variables and this really is the y-degree. And the ordinary regularity of the flattened ideal is 10, which coincides with the file's guessed p = 10 but is a different invariant -- the guess is about the y-regularity of the special fiber, while betti(C, Weights => {1,1,1,1,0,0,0,0,0}) gives 19 for the Rees algebra. One thing I could not reproduce and am not calling a defect: the file's loop 'for i from 4 to 10 do ... 0==compress(basis(i+j, R^1) % L^i)', annotated 'and there it's ok', prints false at every i for me. L is ideal random(R^1, R^{4:-1}), so my L is not his, the file records no expected output, and the whole loop is a genericity check.

the file is a working snapshot of the SchurFunctors package under development -- its first eleven lines are the newPackage declaration commented out so the file can be loaded directly -- and the crash is in draft code that the shipped package does not share. On the file's own E2a for hessian, a 66-by-227 presentation, LinearAlgebra returns 660 generators and the same module as the default, in 1.14 s against the default's 5.73 s -- and the same with the two runs in the opposite order, and on twelve random module Groebner bases over ZZ/32003[a..e], and on K4's E2a. Its timing notes: 'time gens gb presentation E2; -- 13.63 sec on MBP' is 5.73 s here, and 'time annihilator E2; -- 9038 seconds on habanero' is 1165.71 s with Strategy => Quotient, giving 427 generators. That 427 is the confirmation that this is the same computation the file recorded, because its otherwise unlabelled betti comment reads 'total: 1 427'; note the comment attributes it to EPY(K4), which cannot be right, since K4 gives an annihilator of 16 generators in 0.236 s. unmet, and the ask is ambiguous in the place that decides how hard it is. Three lines: 'it would be good if the engine (and front end) could be asked for the space occupied by an object, and the computation would take into account multiple pointers that happen to point to the same space.' Nothing provides it today: engineMemory() reports engine-wide slab size, stash space and finalization counts for GB and res objects, not per-object figures; size2 is the bit length of an integer; there is no allocatedBytes or memoryUsage. The ambiguity is the clause about shared pointers, which could mean either the bytes reachable only from this object -- what you would free by dropping it -- or the bytes reachable at all, and for shared structure those differ a lot. libgc offers GC_size for a single allocated block, so the first half is cheap and the sharing-aware total is a heap traversal M2 would have to write, with the choice between the two quantities made first. Nobody has asked in the seventeen years since. Not filed on those grounds, and reversible cheaply if anyone wants it: the natural consumer is leak hunting, which currently substitutes RSS deltas -- bugs/anton/MEMORY-LEAKS/test-mem-leaks.m2 shells out to ps -o rss and divides by the iteration count, and every leak row in this catalogue was settled with it. one of six files that are a single artefact: Yang-Hui He's Groebner benchmark of M2 against Singular, March 2008, sent because Mike asked for it -- 'Could you email me some GB examples where singular is much faster (and gives an answer) than M2?'. The claim is one sentence, 'the GB ccomputation is about twice as fast for singular.. and this goes on for more complicated examples', with no numbers. Measured it properly, both systems on the same ideal, 66 generators of degree 4 in 48 variables, and every run below returns an identical Groebner basis of 4761 elements: Singular 4.3.2 takes 0.061 s over ZZ/101 and 0.066 s over QQ; M2 1.26.06 takes 31.4 s with gb over ZZ/101, 34.0 s with gb over QQ, 19.0 s with Algorithm => Homogeneous2 over QQ, 3.22 s with groebnerBasis(..., Strategy => "MGB"), and 540 s with Strategy => "F4". So the gap today is about 50-fold at M2's best and 500-fold by default, not twofold. Settled wontfix across the cluster on the maintainer's call: M2 gets the right answer, nothing in the files is asserted to be wrong, and closing a general GB performance gap against another system is not a defect with a closing condition. Two M2-internal facts in that table are worth someone's attention if this is ever revisited, and neither needs Singular to state: gb is ten times slower than the MGB reducer that groebnerBasis already exposes, and Strategy => "F4" is seventeen times slower than gb's own default. Note also that the two coefficient fields differ between the files as stored -- the Singular listing says ring S = 0 (QQ) while the M2 listing has kk = ZZ/101 active and --kk = QQ commented out -- so a naive side-by-side compares different computations; here it barely matters, 31.4 against 34.0 s. Searched titles and bodies for Singular, faster, slow and Groebner: no issue tracks this comparison. This is the follow-up message of 25 March 2008, nine days after the first, offering 'another (from super-QCD (5,4) )' from the same family; its code is bugs/mike/1-yang-2nd.m2, settled in the previous batch. Nothing in it is a separate claim.

in the yang cluster by name only: not Yang's benchmark but Mike's own two experimental implementations, subring1 and subring2, for presenting the subring generated by a ring map, over kk = QQ with R = kk[X_{1}..X_{13}] modulo thirteen fterms and S = kk[y_{1}..y_{22}]. This copy is broken, and the fault is in the bugs/ tree rather than in Singular or M2: the Singular code was extracted from the quoted-printable email body without decoding it, leaving 105 lines that end in a bare '=' soft break and resume mid-token, so the variable X_16 appears as 'X' at the end of one line and '_16' at the start of the next. the file asks its own question in its first line -- 'Is there a bug here? I'm not sure.' -- and the answer is no, on the one claim it makes. That claim is a commented-out line, '--sort (gens i, DegreeOrder => Descending) this does NOT give the right thing'. Over kk = ZZ/32003[a,b,c,d] with the five-component Degrees and MonomialOrder => {Position => Up, Lex => 4} that the file sets up, and i = ideal"a4d,bd2, bcd, ac2" trimmed, gens i is {b*d^2, b*c*d, a*c^2, a^4*d}. sort with MonomialOrder => Descending gives {a^4*d, a*c^2, b*c*d, b*d^2} and with DegreeOrder => Descending gives {a^4*d, b*d^2, b*c*d, a*c^2}: both put the degree-5 generator first and the three degree-3 ones after, so both are descending by degree, and they differ only in how the three-way tie at degree 3 is broken, where DegreeOrder gives exactly the reverse of the monomial-descending order. That is consistent with what the option promises, since sort-doc.m2:123-126 says only that it will 'first order the columns of the matrix in ascending or descending degree' -- degree is the primary key and the tie-break is not specified. Mike appears to have expected ties broken descending too. Otherwise the file runs clean: it needs load "randomIdeal.m2", which is not in the removed bugs tree, not in the catalogue and not anywhere in the repository's history, and with that one line skipped the whole file completes with exit 0 and no errors. Nothing in it is asserted.

two comment lines above an end, then Mike's prototype: 'intersect needs a degree limit -- allow intersect to use: DegreeLimit, Strategy=>Iterative'. still crashes, and it is the first live segfault in this catalogue. Three lines: over B = ZZ[x,y,z], topCoefficients matrix{{x,y},{y^2,x^2},{x^3,y^3}} annotated '-- CRASH!!'. It does, on 1.26.06, and the trigger reduces to two entries -- topCoefficients matrix{{x},{y}} -- with the coefficient ring irrelevant, ZZ, QQ and ZZ/101 all going down. What matters is two or more rows with a component that is present and whose coefficient of the top variable's top power is zero: {{x},{x}} is fine because both components involve x, {{x},{0}} is fine because a zero entry is absent from the sparse vector, and any one-row matrix is fine because the loop body runs once. Cause read off the source rather than guessed. Ring::make_vec returns a null pointer for a zero coefficient (rings/ring-vecs.cpp:22), and PolyRing::vec_coefficient_of_var does vec_result->next = make_vec(t->comp, head.next) followed by vec_result = vec_result->next, so vec_result becomes null and the next iteration dereferences it; the stack trace agrees, vec_coefficient_of_var at rings/poly.cpp:2366 under Matrix::top_coefficients at matrices/matrix.cpp:1009 under rawTopCoefficients. The same assumption was fixed next door two months ago: #4429's commit d8548bd18a wraps the equivalent append in coeffs_of_vec with if (v != nullptr), so this is a missed instance of a pattern already recognised in the same file, and that diff is the model for the fix. Not #162, which is titled 'topCoefficients crashes easily' but reports topCoefficients matrix {{1}}, the no-variables case that vec_top_coefficient guards with if (x == n_vars()) return v; that one is genuinely fixed -- it now raises 'expected polynomial ring' from factor.m2:218, and matrix{{1_R}} in a polynomial ring returns normally. Searched titles and bodies for topCoefficients, top coefficient, coefficient, SIGSEGV and segfault, and comments for topCoefficients, vec_coefficient_of_var, make_vec and rawTopCoefficients; nothing else touches it.

the ungraceful overflow is now graceful, and the slowness is not a defect. Eight lines: over ZZ/32003[x,y,z], M = matrix{{x^1000000000,y^1000000000,z^1000000000}}, then gbTrace=3, res(coker M, Strategy=>2), and syz M followed by syz oo under the comment 'This is also a monomial overflow situation: which it finds, perhaps not so gracefully.' It finds it gracefully now. syz M succeeds, returning source degree 2e = 2000000000, which still fits int32; syz syz M raises 'error: monomial exponent overflow: int32_t + int32_t' from gb.m2:196 in 0.0003 sec, a trapped and specific error rather than a crash, from the safe:: overflow work. res(coker M, Strategy=>2) does not reach that check -- it allocates until the heap cap is hit -- and I first read that as a defect on the grounds that cost grows linearly in e (0.0018, 0.0097, 0.149 sec at e = 10^3, 10^4, 10^5) while Strategy=>0 stays flat (0.0011, 0.0016, 0.0024) and the answer is ranks {1,3,3,1} for every e. That inference was wrong. The resolution's free modules are generated in degrees 0, e, 2e, 3e -- syz M returning degree 2e confirms the middle one -- so its degree range is genuinely Theta(e), and a degree-by-degree algorithm must make Theta(e) passes. Strategy=>0 is flat because it is a different algorithm that does not iterate over degrees at all, not a better degree loop, so its speed here is not evidence against the others. Both Complexes and OldChainComplexes grow the same way, with only a steady 1.3-1.6x factor between them, so this is also not #4278. Nothing to file.

Dan's suggestions were taken, six months after he made them. A 74-line July 2006 mail thread on monomial packing making three points: the union pack4 wastes half of each word if long is ever 64 bits, so use fixed-width types; MO_pack4's nested if-statements break the pipeline and could be unrolled; and w.i = expon[0] | expon[1] << 8 | ... would store to memory once instead of four times. Commit 1a48bb1ab2 (Mike, 2007-01-07, 'dan's changes to packing of monomials') deleted the union and its two endian variants outright and rewrote MO_pack4 and MO_pack2 in exactly the shift-and-or form Dan sketched, one store per slot. The current e/imonorder.cpp:345-361 is that code, now with safe::fits_7 guarding each byte, and it declares int32_t rather than long, so the 64-bit concern cannot arise; util/targettypes.h, which Dan pointed at, no longer exists because the standard fixed-width types replaced it. The thread's closing question, what MonomialSize=>64 would mean, is a separate matter from the packing and not a defect. Nothing to file.

the two-argument reesIdeal cannot finish here, and the cause is the ring presentation it saturates in. Seventeen lines, headed 'Add these examples to the ReesAlgebra benchmark code', holding two examples with recorded times. The first: i = monomialCurveIdeal(S,{4,8,11,13,15}) in ZZ/101[a..g], with reesIdeal(i) at 1.7 sec and reesIdeal(i,i_0) commented out as 'doesn't finish before I get impatient (10 min?)'. Both still hold on 1.26.06 -- reesIdeal i returns 24 generators in 1.94 sec, and reesIdeal(i, i_0) was killed at 15 min. i_0 = e^2-d*f is a nonzero element of a domain so the method's non-zerodivisor precondition is met. Broke the cost down: trim is free at 0.0008 and 0.0003 sec, symmetricAlgebraIdeal takes 56.8 sec, and the saturate that follows exceeds 180 sec. The saturation runs in S[w_0..w_7], a tower whose coefficientRing is S, so isFlatPolynomialRing at Saturation.m2:72 is false, and the checks at Saturation.m2:533, 555 and 579 make Linear, Bayer, GRevLex and Eliminate all decline in under a millisecond, leaving only the naive Iterate. Flatten the ring first and change nothing else and the same saturation returns in 9.9 sec with the same 24 generators. So the difference is between not finishing and finishing, caused by the library handing saturate a shape that disables its good strategies. Two honest limits on this. In the flat ring, explicit Eliminate and explicit Iterate each also exceeded 300 sec while the default chain took 9.9 sec, so I cannot say which strategy wins there and the issue says so. And even flattened the two-argument form would total about 67 sec against 1.94, so the 'usually faster' comment above the method still fails on this example -- the file's second example, ideal random(S^1,S^{-3,-4,-5,-6}) in four variables, runs the other way at 8.4 versus 1.4 sec. Written against the draft package in ReesAlgebra2.m2, which is itself obsolete, but the methods and the behaviour carried over to the shipped ReesAlgebra. Searched titles and bodies for reesIdeal, ReesAlgebra, symmetricKernel, symmetricAlgebraIdeal, saturate, flattenRing, tower and isFlatPolynomialRing, and comments for reesIdeal; #4308 is a different saturate method and the open flattenRing issues are about flattenRing itself, not about callers that fail to use it.

this is a timing example for #4590, which I filed earlier in this effort from bugs/dan/1-kernel-ringmap. Fourteen lines: R = ZZ/32003 in 5 variables, S in 6, phi = map(R,S,random(R^1,R^{6:-2})), gbTrace=3, then ker phi and betti oo, followed by the same thing with named variables a..f and A..G and a bare syz phi.matrix. It carries no comment and asserts nothing, which is why it reads at first like a pure benchmark; the harness records autorun=timeout. What makes it a duplicate is that its map's source variables have degree 1 while their images are quadrics, so nothing in sight is homogeneous, and #4590's body identifies the inhomogeneous case as the one that is unmet: canUseHilbertHint requires isHomogeneous (gb.m2:271), so with standard degrees the graph ideal is inhomogeneous, the hint block is skipped, and there is no homogenize/dehomogenize path of the kind Mike's 2008 email asked for. Tied the timing to that exact predicate rather than to a resemblance. Regrading S with Degrees => {6:2} leaves the kernel the same set of polynomials and changes only whether the algorithm can see the map as graded: with standard degrees isHomogeneous phi false, graph inhomogeneous, canUseHilbertHint false, and ker phi did not finish in 600 sec; with S's variables in degree 2, all three true, and ker phi returned in 196 sec as a single generator of degree 32, the degree-16 implicit equation of the image hypersurface. Two limits on what that pair proves. 600 sec is a lower bound since it never finished. And regrading buys homogeneity in general, not only the hint -- a graded Groebner basis also gains degree-by-degree progress and early termination -- so 196 versus 600 bounds the prize for implementing the homogenize/dehomogenize path from above rather than measuring it. Note also that my first write-up of this row justified the duplicate by quoting #4590's title, 'unless the map preserves degrees', which is shorthand; the argument above rests on the body instead. Two traps worth recording for anyone re-running this: vars(26..31) is A..F, so a matrix named F is silently clobbered when S is created -- the original file avoids this only by inlining the matrix into map -- and in M2 an else on its own line ends the statement.

a debugging methodology note plus a root-cause diagnosis, and the bug it diagnoses is fixed. 110 lines: first a numbered list of what Mike had to arrange to debug libfac through M2 -- build with debug symbols, keep gdb settings out of .emacs, use Linux because gdb on macOS was useless at the time, call showcf and showcfl from x-factor.cpp, and define IRRCHARSERIESDEBUG and CERR in charset.cc. Then a February 2013 email to Hans Schoenemann carrying the same ideal as decompose5.m2 and, after 'several long sessions' with gdb, an actual diagnosis: IrrCharSeries walks its computation tree depth-first over a TODO list qhi, and the optimization that memoizes already-seen characteristic sets in the set 'pi' prunes wrongly. At loop 4 a char set is added to pi under a branch where (v2+1)(v6+1)=0 forces v6+1=0; at loop 113 the same char set comes up under a weaker branch, is found already in pi, so its initial set is never added, v5-1 never enters the ideal, and the whole subtree where v6+1 is not in the minimal prime is lost -- which is exactly the three missing minimal primes. Line 28 records that this 'was supposedly fixed in libfac-3-1-6'. It was: decompose5.m2 and decompose6.m2 both verify correct output on 1.26.06, including through rawCharSeries directly. The scaffolding the note describes is also gone -- e/x-factor.cpp no longer exists, the interface is e/interface/factory.cpp, and M2 links an external factory rather than a bundled libfac, so charset.cc is not in this tree to edit. Kept in git history for whoever next needs to read IrrCharSeries. Nothing to file.

decompose is right now, and so is the char series underneath it. The file is a 2013 regression test whose comment reads 'the decompose is WRONG!': it carries a 19-component reference decomposition of an 11-generator ideal in QQ[v7..v1] with Lex order, produced by the then-new PD package, and asserts that decompose reproduces it. In September 2013 it did not -- Mike recorded three components missing and four spurious ones, and both #C1 from rawCharSeries and #C2 from decompose as wrong. On 1.26.06 every one of those checks passes. Compared as sets of Groebner bases against the 19-component reference: decompose 19 and equal, minimalPrimes default 19 and equal, minimalPrimes Strategy=>Birational 19 and equal, and minimalPrimes Strategy=>Legacy 19 and equal -- Legacy being the path that still goes through irreducibleCharacteristicSeries and hence rawCharSeries at MinimalPrimes.m2:364. rawCharSeries called directly returns 19 series. So this is not merely decompose having been rerouted around a broken component; the char series itself is fixed. See debugging-singular-code, which diagnoses the cause in libfac's IrrCharSeries, and decompose6.m2, which is the same defect reduced. The fix is upstream in factory rather than in this tree, which is why no commit here can be named. Nothing to file.

the crash is gone and the two strategies now agree. Fourteen lines from G.G. Smith: over KK = QQ[r]/cyclotomicPoly(3,r) and S = KK[x_0..x_11], build a 9x9 block matrix from a diagonal block A scaled by powers of r and a generic 3x3 block B, then det(M, Strategy=>Bareiss) annotated 'crashes' against det(M, Strategy=>Cofactor) annotated 'OK'. On 1.26.06 Bareiss returns: 1147 terms of degree 9, identical to Cofactor's answer, and det A is the expected degree-3 form. The interesting part is the setting rather than the size -- Bareiss is fraction-free elimination and needs exact division, and the coefficient ring here is a quotient of a polynomial ring that M2 is not told is a field, which is the usual way that strategy gets into trouble. I could not name the fix: there is no commit whose message mentions Bareiss since 2013, and the plausible candidates in e/det.cpp are restructurings and clang-format runs rather than behaviour changes, so this was most likely repaired indirectly in the coefficient-ring arithmetic. Nothing to file.

a performance wish, and its body is unreachable. 41 lines whose first two are the whole claim -- 'This is an example that Bernd Sturmfels asked about and it would be nice to improve its performance' -- followed by `end` on line 4, so nothing after it executes and the harness records autorun=pass-partial for a file that in effect does nothing. The example itself is the maximum likelihood degree setup for a 4-by-4 symmetric matrix: Xad the adjugate built from ten 3-by-3 minors, Model1 = ideal(A * Xad) for a random 5-by-10 integer A, then gens gb(Model1, Algorithm=>LinearAlgebra), a colon by minors(3,X), and dim and degree of the result. Note that the Algorithm=>LinearAlgebra it reaches for is the same option devel-f4-eg1.m2 measures, where it is about twice as slow in wall time as the default on a 32-variable example, so this file's instinct that that setting would help is not obviously right. a developer scratchpad for the linear-algebra Groebner engine; everything it exercises still works. 190 lines of small trials over ZZ/101 and ZZ/32003, mostly gens gb with Algorithm=>LinearAlgebra, several passing GBDegrees to weight the variables and one passing Strategy=>UseSyzygies, interspersed with collectGarbage and gbRemove to reset state between runs. No claim that any answer is wrong and no recorded timings to check. Verified the options are all still live on 1.26.06: Algorithm=>LinearAlgebra with GBDegrees=>{1,1,1} and Strategy=>UseSyzygies returns the same 3 elements as the default on ideal random(R^1,R^{-2,-2}) in three variables, GBDegrees with a monomial ideal in four variables gives 5, and the plain LinearAlgebra runs on ideal(a*b*c,b*c*d,c*d*e) in six. One thing turned up that the file does not report and that I did not file, on Doug's instruction to raise it on #4518 instead: the sibling option Algorithm=>ParallelF4 is exported and accepted by gb but fails on every input I tried, down to ideal(a^2-b*c,a*b) in ZZ/101[a,b,c], with 'error: unknown engine error' from gb.m2:200, and before failing it prints engine hash-table debug output to stdout with gbTrace unset. It is undocumented -- only m2/exports.m2:323, the dispatch at m2/gb.m2:137 commented 'also experimental', and the authors' own e/gb-f4/testing.m2 -- and e/gb-f4 was last touched 2026-06-02 with commits reading 'compiles', so the engine is mid-construction and its being unfinished is not news to anyone. What is worth raising is that unlike Toric, which calls warnexp() at m2/gb.m2:87, it gives no experimental warning, so from a released M2 it looks as legitimate as LinearAlgebra. See devel-f4-eg1.m2, which carries the #4518 comment. Nothing to file.

the capability this prototype was reaching for now exists in the engine. Its first two lines are the whole context: 'This code is experimental, and probably old. Still, it might be useful. Trying to get fraction field GB's working well... at least 0-dimensional ones.' 225 lines: an 8-generator ideal from the primary decomposition examples over ZZ/32003, then a hand-written spoly and a Buchberger loop operating over a localization, doing the coefficient arithmetic by hand with sub(leadCoefficient f, R) and syz(matrix{{a,b}}, SyzygyLimit=>1). Corrected on re-examination: I first filed this obsolete and wrote that fraction-field Groebner bases remain a real gap. They do not. Over K = frac(ZZ/32003[b,c,g]) and R = K[a,d,f,h,e], with coefficientRing R === K confirmed, gens gb of a five-generator ideal returns 8 elements, dim is 0 and the quotient has a 4-element basis; a second, plainly 0-dimensional ideal in the same ring gives 5 elements and dim 0. So the engine handles exactly the case the file set out to reach, and by the ordinary gb interface rather than by the hand-rolled loop here. That makes this fixed rather than merely superseded, though there is no single commit to name -- the support came in with the engine's frac handling, not as a fix for this file. The related dispatch question, how gb should reach alternative Groebner engines at all, is live in #4518. Nothing to file.

a debugging scratchpad whose features all still work; it cannot run past line 21. 32 lines headed 'Debugging of binomial and toric GB's': gens gb of ideal(a^2-b*c, a*b-c*d) over ZZ/101[a..f] both plainly and with Algorithm=>Toric, then an assocModel helper building the A matrix of an m-by-n association model, then LLL syz of it and a toric GB in 16 and 20 variables. Checked the pieces on 1.26.06: Algorithm=>Toric is still accepted and returns the same 3 elements as the default on the small example, though it now emits 'warning: gb algorithm requested is experimental' from m2/gb.m2:87 -- Toric is the only Algorithm value that warns. the answer to 'Is this a bug in linalg gb?' is no, and finding that out required measuring wall clock rather than cpu. 53 lines: a 29-generator binomial ideal in the 32 variables p_(1,1,1,1,1)..p_(2,2,2,2,2) over ZZ/32003 with MonomialSize=>8, ending in two timings, gb with Algorithm=>LinearAlgebra at 59.7 sec and plain gb at 21.6 sec on the author's 2008 MacBook Pro, under the header question. On 1.26.06 both still return the same 3626 element basis, and in wall time LinearAlgebra takes 44 sec against the default's 21 -- a factor of 2.2, where in 2008 it was 2.8. So the ratio, which is the only hardware-independent quantity here, has if anything improved slightly; there is no regression and an F4-style method losing to Buchberger on a particular input is expected rather than defective. My first measurement said 10x, because I timed with cpuTime and LinearAlgebra has been parallel since #3554 (merged Oct 2024); its cpu is 178 sec against 44 sec wall. Setting allowableThreads=1 did not change either number, so that option does not gate this strategy. Surveying the neighbouring routes produced the thing actually worth reporting, so this row carries a comment on #4518 rather than an issue: on the same input groebnerBasis(J, Strategy=>"MGB") returns the same basis in 4 sec wall, five times faster than the default and 43 times faster than groebnerBasis(J, Strategy=>"F4") at 173 sec, and MGB is not among the values processAlgorithm accepts at m2/gb.m2:118-139, so gb cannot select it. That 173-versus-44 gap also answers the TODO at m2/gb.m2:113-117 asking whether groebnerBasis's "F4" is the same as Algorithm=>LinearAlgebra: it is not. Searched titles and bodies for LinearAlgebra, F4, linalg, Groebner and gb, and ParallelF4; #3554 is the parallelism PR, #2162 and #4386 are mathicgb F4 on s390x and 32-bit ARM, and nothing covers the algorithm-surface question.

a hand-rolled Groebner walk, superseded by a shipped package. 305 lines of prototype: parallelLeadTerms wrapping rawGBGetParallelLeadTerms, a bd helper forming normalized exponent differences, dmon, and a computeNextW whose own comment says it 'does the case grevlex --> lex'. No claim that anything in M2 is wrong -- this is Mike working out the algorithm, not reporting a defect. It has been a distributed package since d7a45d9a3a, 'Add new package GroebnerWalk v1.0.0' by Dylan Peifer, 2017-11-17, which exports groebnerWalk, setWalkTrace and getWalkTrace and whose documentation describes exactly the motivation in this file: get a basis over a hard order such as lex by walking from an easy one such as grevlex. It is still maintained -- c91b23a82a (kellerlv, 2026-05-20) added seven tests to it. The engine hook the prototype leans on, rawGBGetParallelLeadTerms, is still present in the Core private dictionary, so the file would still run, but there is no reason to prefer it. Nothing to file.

the author says outright it is not a bug, and it cannot run as written. Line 1: 'This is not a bug, but an example, see Frietag, 1506.00892v1.pdf'. 36 lines building the Freitag example over ZZ/32003[y_0..y_3, x_0..x_3] -- four generators y_i^2 minus signed sums of x_j^2, then the singular locus via trim(I + minors(4, jacobian I)), decompose of it, the degree-4 part phi, and a 2-by-2 minor construction in P^7 x P^57 requiring a 66-variable ring, ending in minprimes with Verbosity=>2, a Groebner basis of a saturation, and codim checks. Two reasons it fails rather than merely being slow: factorize on lines 24 and 31 is not a function and never was one -- searching all of history for a definition under m2/ or packages/ finds nothing, so this is not a removal. The spelling the file wanted is factors, from MinimalPrimes (MinimalPrimes.m2:428), which the file already loads and which returns the (multiplicity, factor) pairs its code destructures as v#1: factors((x^2-y^2)*(x+1)) gives {(1,x+1), (1,x-y), (1,x+y)}. So the file was never runnable as typed -- and the file's numbered claims are annotations of a paper's construction, not expectations of M2. The restart on line 2 is a no-op under --script, which is why an earlier pass of this triage misread this file's status; see the README section on --script and stdin failing in opposite directions. Nothing to file.

more test data, and the one timing claim in it no longer holds. 40 lines, four blocks. med1-ZZ is ideal((3x+y+z+w)^4, (7x+2y+3z)^4+xw^3, (x+y+z)^4) over ZZ[x,y,z,w] with Lex order, carrying a single enormous test'code string that asserts the exact leadTerm of the basis, coefficients up to 10^60 included. elim1 is an 8-generator inhomogeneous system in 9 variables over ZZ/32003, preceded by six discarded ring declarations -- including R = K[a,d,f,h,e] over K = frac(ZZ/32003[b,c,g]), which is the fraction-field experiment of devel-1-fracgb.m2 -- and annotated twice 'this runs very quickly, where the inhomog version grounds to a halt'. It does not grind: on 1.26.06 gens gb of the inhomogeneous ideal takes 0.155 sec against 0.009 sec homogenized, a factor of 17 on a computation that is instant either way, and both give 26 elements. The neighbouring note 'time decompose I -- .45 seconds' is now 2.5 sec for 8 components, but that is a different machine and a rewritten minimal primes implementation, so it proves nothing either way. Two things in the file no longer exist: rad, which line 29 reaches for via debug PrimaryDecomposition, is gone in favour of radical in Core, and the lichtblau-32003 and lichtblau-QQ blocks need ExampleIdeals, which fecbbf8aef (Dan, 2020-07-08) moved into packages/undistributed-packages, so it is present in the tree but not installed and needsPackage fails. Nothing to file.

a Groebner basis regression suite, and it still passes in full. 178 lines, 26 blocks separated by dashed rules, each naming an example and setting a ring, an ideal I, and usually an expected answer'gb, with occasional answer'mingens and test'code. Rather than classify it unrun I split it into blocks and checked each against its recorded answer, comparing both the ideal and the sorted generator list: 23 of the 23 blocks that carry an answer'gb reproduce it exactly, 0 failures. That includes the delicate ones -- the five ZZ examples simple21 through simple25 with their integer content and Lex orders, where simple23 expects the constant 24336 in the basis, and trim-32003 whose test'code asserts g0 == g2 after a trim round-trip. The three blocks with no expected answer are simple7, labelled 'semi-random', and the two Hilbert-function examples simple19-hf and simple20-hf, which produce 82, 17 and 94 elements. So there is nothing wrong here; the file is test data whose companion runner is the separate row run-gb-test-examples.m2. I first wrote that these 23 checks could be promoted into tests/normal. Withdrawn: this README argues at length that when a reproducer was worth keeping the maintainers moved it at the time -- which is exactly what happened to 1-mingens-subquotient.m2 and 1-joswig, both promoted by their own fix commits -- and that inventing a test disposition twenty years later is not the same act. The disposition is drop; the file stays in git history, which is where it is useful. Nothing to file.

Conway's Game of Life as a Boolean Groebner basis problem, a technique demonstration rather than a defect report. 158 lines with `end` at line 72, so the half that runs is definitions only. Those definitions are the interesting part: booleanRing n builds ZZ/2[vars(0..n-1)] under Lex modulo the field equations x^2+x, and doMyExample compares three routes to the same basis -- gens gb with Algorithm=>Sugarless and Strategy=>LongPolynomial in a GRevLex copy of the ring, then poincare of the forced lead-term basis to obtain a Hilbert function, then a Hilbert-driven gb in a homogenized Lex ring -- timing each of the three stages separately. After `end` come the life-transition ideals themselves and, in GameOfLifeSimple.m2, a solution printed as an explicit hash table of variable-to-bit assignments. Both files reference gbBoolean from the BooleanGB package, which is still present in packages/ and is the subject of #4518's complaint that it exports a separate entry point instead of registering a strategy gb would find. No assertion, no recorded timing to compare against, and no claim that M2 gets anything wrong. The directory is Mike's March 2010 benchmark harness for the gbB Groebner engine refactor, and gbB itself no longer exists -- nothing in e/ mentions it, the engine's Buchberger class being gbA in groebner-computations/gb-default.hpp. So the refactor these files were built to measure finished long ago and took its subject with it. Nothing to file.

the example collection for the harness: a superset of a file M2 still carries, and revivable with a two-token substitution. 380 lines of large Groebner benchmarks -- yang1, a 48-variable ideal from Yang-Hui He related to string theory, then random5555, random5556, 40vars, gbB148, hilbert-kunz-1, mayr42, assocModel45, chow-flag-7-7-over-h, a parametric resultant example, and kleinberg1, the last cross-referencing bugs/mike/0-kleinberg. Each carries recorded comparisons in a block comment, which is where the value is: for yang1, LinearAlgebra 69.9 sec, Sugarless with Strategy=>LongPolynomial 66.0, Homogeneous2 with LongPolynomial 43.8, MaxReductionCount=>3000 51.34, plus engine-internal breakdowns such as 'total time for making matrix (includes sort): 38.583083' and 'total time for gauss: 18.888364'. the leak is still live, but its tracker is #488, not the #468 in the filename. 143 lines from 23 May 2016 wrapping Christian Bopp's example in leak1 and variants: over T = ZZ/12347[t_0..t_8], generate 100 random genus-9 canonical curves and for each take betti(res(IC, FastNonminimal=>true), Minimize=>true), discarding the result and reassigning IC. #468, 'memory leak in fast nonminimal resolution code', was closed 2016-05-29; Dan opened #488 on 2016-06-16 with the same loop written with minimalBetti, probing whether IC.cache.quotient was the retainer and calling the outcome 'totally perplexing'. #488 is still open, so that is where this belongs. Two things had to be fixed before it could even be measured: RandomCanonicalCurves has been merged into RandomCurves, and FastNonminimal is no longer an option of the default res, the current spelling being Strategy=>Nonminimal. My first attempt reported identical memory at N=5, 20 and 40 -- that was a process dying immediately on the unknown option, which the suspiciously constant wall times gave away. Measured properly, as peak RSS at N=20 against N=200 with everything else held fixed: generating curves alone 309.3 then 310.1 MB, flat; adding gens gb IC per curve 309.3 then 310.2 MB, still flat; adding minimalBetti IC 333.7 then 499.0 MB, about 0.92 MB per iteration; the same with Dan's IC.cache.quotient = null 333.7 then 500.2 MB, 0.93; and the file's own res(Strategy=>Nonminimal) plus betti(Minimize=>true) 355.9 then 686.3 MB, 1.83 MB per iteration, growing linearly across a fortyfold range from N=5 to N=200 with no plateau. The gb control is the useful one: it caches on the same ideals in the same ring and does not grow, which rules out both ring accumulation and caching on the ideal as such, leaving the nonminimal resolution itself. And the cache.quotient assignment changes nothing, which answers the question Dan was actually stuck on. Caveats: peak RSS is a high-water mark and Boehm does not return pages, so this measures heap demand rather than live data, and I did not establish whether the memory is unreachable-but-uncollected or reachable-but-retained. Searched titles for memory leak, leak, Nonminimal and nonminimal resolution, and bodies for memory leak and Strategy=>Nonminimal; #424 and #469 are other 2016 nonminimal issues, both closed, and #3068 is a caching-versus-Minimize error rather than a leak.

The capability is very much alive: m2/gb.m2:390 calls the five argument form, which is what groebnerBasis(I, Strategy=>"MGB") uses, and on the first block's ideal the comparison the file wanted holds, the MGB lead terms equalling gb's as sets. Two further reasons it could not run as written: block 2 needs ExampleIdeals, undistributed since fecbbf8aef, and block 3's last line compares against leadTerm gb I1 where the ideal it built is J1, so that line was broken when written. Worth knowing that MGB is the fastest route on yang1 by a wide margin -- 4 sec against the default's 21 -- which is recorded on #4518 from devel-f4-eg1.m2. Nothing to file.

a 2010 package draft, not a bug report. 39 lines declaring newPackage "oneStep3" dated March 10 2010 with DebuggingMode => true, exporting a single method: iteration(Ring,List,Ideal) takes a ring, a list of ideals giving the split subvarieties of some dimension, and one ideal from that list, then intersects it with the others and decomposes, finds the non-R1 locus as the codimension-one part of decompose ideal singularLocus(R/I), computes ideal integralClosure(R/I) with its icFractions, maps the divisor into the new ring and returns the tuple. That is one step of an algorithm for compatibly split subvarieties, Frobenius splitting work; the header comment describes inputs and outputs and nothing else. `end` sits on the last line, so even the package body would not load past it in the usual paste-a-block workflow. a hand-rolled univariate root finder, and M2 now ships the function. 81 lines building it from parts: toCoefficients pulls the dense coefficient list of a polynomial in one variable via coefficients(F, Monomials=>...), eval does Horner evaluation for both a coefficient list and a polynomial, companionMatrix assembles the companion matrix as a mutableMatrix over the coefficient ring, roots takes its eigenvalues, and polishRoots does Newton refinement to a requested precision. No assertion, no complaint about M2 -- it is an implementation. It is superseded: roots is a shipped function on 1.26.06, and roots(x^2-2) over QQ[x] returns {1.41421, -1.41421}. Nothing to file.
